Creamy dips (ranch, blue cheese)1 cup~100–170 cal
Garlic / butter dips1 cupHighest — check in app

Two lava cakes plus two ranch cups is about 1,040 calories of things you'd probably describe as "just a bit extra." If you love a dip — and I do — marinara is the freebie. It's a fraction of the creamy ones and it goes with everything on the menu.

Don't Forget the Drink

A 20 oz bottle of regular soda is roughly 240 calories, which is very close to an entire extra slice of large cheese pizza. Diet or zero-sugar versions are effectively zero, and bottled water obviously is. Nothing else on this page gives you a ~240-calorie saving for so little sacrifice. Our Domino's drinks guide has the full lineup.

The Lowest-Calorie Domino's Order

Put it all together and here's what a genuinely light order looks like, without pretending you're eating salad:

  • Medium Crunchy Thin, light cheese, veggie toppings — around 130–150 calories a slice
  • Two slices, not four — roughly 300 calories total
  • Marinara instead of ranch — saves ~125 calories a cup
  • A zero-sugar drink — saves ~240 calories
  • Skip the bread bowl, keep the pasta dish — saves ~350–400

That's a real dinner around the 400-calorie mark. Compare it with a casual default order — three large pepperoni slices, half an order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread, ranch and a regular soda — which clears 2,000. Same restaurant, same twenty minutes, five times the calories.

Seven Ways to Cut Calories Without Hating Your Order

None of these require willpower. They're just menu mechanics.

  • Switch to Crunchy Thin. Same price, same toppings, ~500 fewer calories on a large.
  • Ask for light cheese. It's a free modification and it trims 20–30 calories a slice without making the pizza taste bare.
  • Swap one meat for one veg. Pepperoni to peppers is a real cut and the pizza still tastes loaded.
  • Order the size you'll eat, not the size that's cheapest. A large is better value, but only if the extra slices aren't eaten out of proximity.
  • Box the leftovers before you sit down. The fourth slice is almost never hunger.
  • Make the side a starter, not an addition. Wings or cheesy bread, with one fewer slice.
  • Let the drink do the work. Zero-sugar. It's the cheapest 240 calories you'll ever save.

If the goal is trimming the bill as well as the calorie count, the same "order on purpose" logic applies — our money-saving playbook and the current Domino's coupons page cover that side.

How to Check Exact Calories Before You Order

Every number on this page is a guide. Here's how to get the real one for the exact pizza you're about to buy:

  • Build it in the app or on the site. Domino's Cal-O-Meter recalculates as you add and remove toppings, so you see the effect of every choice before you pay.
  • Read the per-slice figure, not the whole-pizza one. Menus often show the pizza total, which looks alarming until you divide by eight.
  • Check the published nutrition guide for sides. Sides and dips vary more between versions than pizzas do.
  • Ask the store about preparation. Useful for allergens especially — the gluten-free crust is prepared in a shared kitchen, so it suits a preference rather than celiac disease.

How to Read These Numbers

I'd rather be straight with you than look authoritative. Third-party calorie charts for Domino's disagree with each other, sometimes by 30 or 40 calories a slice, because portioning is done by hand, toppings vary, sizes get cut differently and recipes get updated. The figures here are rounded, cross-checked against published nutrition data, and meant for planning, not tracking to the gram.

What doesn't change is the shape of the data, and that's the genuinely useful part: thin beats thick, veggie beats meat, dish beats bread bowl, marinara beats ranch, and the drink matters more than you'd think. Get those five right and the exact number stops being something you need to worry about. Browse the full lineup with example prices on our Domino's menu with prices page, and check the app for the final word on both.

title: Which Domino's Deal Is Actually Cheapest? (2026): We Did the Maths
excerpt: Mix & Match, $6.99 Each, the carryout special, 50% off — Domino's presents them all as great value and never compares them. Here is the arithmetic, scenario by scenario, including the trap that makes the 'better' deal cost you more.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Domino's pizzas and sides laid out, illustrating a comparison of Domino's deals

faqs.question: Which Domino's deal is the cheapest?
faqs.answer: There isn't one, and that's the honest answer. Each deal is built around a different number of items, so the cheapest one depends entirely on how much you're buying. One item is usually the carryout special, two items is Mix & Match, three or more is a $6.99 Each style offer, and a specialty pizza is often cheapest at 50% off menu price.

faqs.question: Is Mix & Match or $6.99 Each better?
faqs.answer: Whichever matches your item count. Mix & Match needs two or more items, $6.99 Each needs three. If you genuinely want three things, the three-item deal wins. If you only want two, adding a third to unlock it costs you about $6.99 to save nothing.

faqs.question: What's the catch with Mix & Match?
faqs.answer: The pizza in it is typically a medium two-topping, not a large. Comparing that price against a large pizza's menu price flatters the deal. It's still good value — you just aren't comparing the same pizza, and it's worth knowing which trade you're making.

faqs.question: Is the carryout special cheaper than delivery deals?
faqs.answer: Almost always, and by more than the headline difference. A carryout price has no delivery fee and no tip attached to it. Adding roughly $5 of fee and $4 of tip to a delivery order makes a $9.99 carryout pizza and a $9.99 delivered pizza about nine dollars apart in practice.

faqs.question: How much does a Domino's deal actually save?
faqs.answer: On our example prices, roughly $3 on a single pizza, $7 on a pizza plus a side, and $13 to $17 on a family-sized order of three to five items. The larger the order, the more the deal structure works in your favour.

faqs.question: Are specialty pizzas included in the deals?
faqs.answer: Not always, and this catches people out. Multi-item offers frequently price around a build-your-own two-topping pizza, with specialty recipes either excluded or carrying an upcharge. When a percentage-off offer is running, that's usually the cheaper route to a specialty pizza.

faqs.question: Can I combine two Domino's deals?
faqs.answer: Generally no. Offers apply one at a time to an order rather than stacking. What you can combine is a deal with carryout and with rewards points, which is effectively three savings on the same order without needing them to stack.

faqs.question: Why do deal prices differ between stores?
faqs.answer: Every Domino's is independently franchised, so stores set their own prices and choose which promotions they take part in. The same deal can be a different price in the next town, and some stores don't run it at all.

faqs.question: What's the single cheapest way to order Domino's?
faqs.answer: Build the largest order you genuinely want inside whichever multi-item deal matches that count, select carryout, and be signed in for rewards points. That combination beats any single tactic, and it costs nothing beyond ten minutes of planning.

faqs.question: Do deals change often?
faqs.answer: Yes. Offers rotate, and the exact price points move. That's why this page is written around the method rather than the numbers — the arithmetic for deciding which deal fits your order stays the same even when the prices don't.

content:
The Answer Nobody Gives You

Domino's runs several deals at once and presents all of them as excellent value. What it never does — and structurally cannot do — is tell you which one is cheapest for the order you're actually placing. So let's do that arithmetic.

The headline finding is not what most people expect. There is no single cheapest deal. Each offer is built around a different number of items, so the right one changes with your basket. The useful question is not "which deal is best" but "how many things am I buying".

Before the numbers: everything below uses example prices, because Domino's stores are franchised and set their own. Offers also rotate. The maths is the point, not the specific figures — plug in whatever your store is showing.

What Each Deal Actually Requires

The requirements matter more than the discounts, because they decide which deals you're even eligible for.

DealMinimum itemsTypical restriction
Large Carryout Special1Carryout only
Mix & Match2Usually a medium 2-topping pizza
$6.99 Each3Qualifying items only
50% off menu price1Menu-price pizzas, limited time
Any-crust style offer1Often excludes specialty recipes

Notice that most deals need more than one item. That single fact explains why a person ordering one pizza often finds nothing applies to them, and it's the first thing to check.

The Maths, Scenario by Scenario

Here's what each situation costs at menu price against the best deal available for it.

What you wantAt menu priceBest dealYou save
1 large pepperoni~$12.99Carryout special ~$9.99~$3.00
Pizza + Stuffed Cheesy Bread~$20.98Mix & Match ~$13.98~$7.00
2 pizzas + a side~$33.97$6.99 Each ~$20.97~$13.00
3 pizzas + side + dessert~$51.95$6.99 Each ~$34.95~$17.00
1 specialty pizza~$16.9950% off ~$8.49~$8.49

Two clear patterns come out of that.

The bigger the order, the harder the deal structure works for you. Three dollars off one pizza is fine; seventeen dollars off a family order is the difference between a cheap dinner and an expensive one. Domino's has deliberately built its pricing to reward larger baskets, and if you're buying a lot anyway, that's genuinely in your favour.

And a single specialty pizza is the odd one out. A percentage-off offer beats the multi-item deals there, because the multi-item deals are priced around a basic two-topping pizza rather than a loaded recipe. More on that below.

The Trap: The Phantom Third Item

This is the part that costs people money, and it's the reason a "better" deal can leave you worse off.

$6.99 Each looks like a stronger offer than Mix & Match — same price per item, and it scales. But it needs three items. So:

What you buyDealTotal
The 2 things you wantedMix & Match~$13.98
Those 2 plus a third to qualify$6.99 Each~$20.97

You didn't save anything. You spent about $6.99 extra to access a lower per-item price on an item you didn't want. The per-item figure went down and the amount leaving your account went up.

This is worth internalising because the app actively nudges toward it — a prompt saying "add one more item to unlock $6.99 each" is technically accurate and financially backwards unless the third item is something you'd have bought anyway.

The test is simple: would you have ordered that third item at any price? If yes, take the deal. If you're adding it only to unlock the offer, you're buying a discount rather than receiving one.

The Mix & Match Asterisk

One honest caveat about the two-item comparison above, because most articles skip it.

The pizza inside Mix & Match is typically a medium two-topping, not a large. So when we compare $13.98 against a $20.98 menu total, part of that gap is a smaller pizza rather than pure discount.

It's still good value — a medium two-topping and a side for fourteen dollars is a decent order. But you should know which trade you're making. If you specifically need a large, price a large inside the deal and check what the upcharge does before assuming the saving holds. Our pizza sizes guide has the per-slice value comparison if you're weighing medium against large.

Carryout Changes Every Number Above

Every figure in this article is a food price. On delivery, that isn't what you pay.

Same $9.99 pizzaWhat it actually costs
Carryout~$9.99
Delivered~$9.99 + ~$5 fee + ~$4 tip = ~$19

That's roughly double, on the identical pizza. Which means the channel decision outranks the deal decision. A mediocre deal on carryout regularly beats the best deal on delivery.

It also means the carryout special isn't really competing with the other offers at all — it's in a different category, because the others don't remove the fee and the tip. Our carryout guide works through that gap in detail, and the tipping guide covers the part of it that goes to the driver.

The Specialty Pizza Exception

If you want an ExtravaganZZa or a Philly Cheese Steak rather than a build-your-own, the usual advice inverts.

Multi-item deals are priced around a two-topping pizza. Specialty recipes carry eight or nine toppings, so they're either excluded from those offers or come with an upcharge that erodes the saving. A percentage-off offer, applied to the specialty's higher menu price, tends to produce the bigger discount — half of $16.99 is a better outcome than a deal that won't take the pizza you want.

There's also a cheaper trick worth knowing: start from a specialty and strip it back. Removing toppings normally costs nothing, so an ExtravaganZZa without the olives is the same price as one with them. Our specialty pizzas guide covers which recipes are which.

Working It Out in Sixty Seconds

You don't need to memorise any of this. The method:

  • Count the items you actually want. Not what unlocks a deal — what you want
  • 1 item: check the carryout special first, and the percentage-off offer if it's a specialty
  • 2 items: Mix & Match
  • 3 or more: the three-item offer, which pulls ahead further as the order grows
  • Then switch it to carryout and look at the total again
  • Be signed in. Rewards points accrue on deal orders too, and they cost nothing to collect

Building the whole order inside one offer, rather than adding items at menu price afterwards, is where most of the saving actually lives.

Mistakes That Cost Real Money

  • Adding a side after applying the deal. It goes on at menu price. Build everything inside the offer
  • Chasing a lower per-item price with items you don't want. The phantom third item, above
  • Assuming your store runs every promotion. Franchises opt in individually — check yours rather than a national advert
  • Comparing a deal price to a large pizza's menu price when the deal is for a medium
  • Taking delivery on a carryout-only special. It isn't available, and the equivalent delivered order is a different price entirely
  • Not checking the deals tab at all. The most expensive way to order is at menu price, and it's also the default

The Short Version

One item: carryout special. Two: Mix & Match. Three or more: the three-item deal. A specialty pizza: percentage off. Then take carryout, and don't add a third item you didn't want just to reach a lower per-item price.

Do that and a family order that would cost around $52 at menu price lands nearer $35 — and around $9 less again once the delivery fee and tip come off. That's roughly a third of the bill, from ten minutes of arithmetic that Domino's has no reason to do on your behalf.

Prices here are examples and deals rotate — check what's live on the current coupons page and confirm at official checkout. For the rest of the levers, see the money-saving playbook and the Mix & Match explainer.

title: Domino's Mix & Match Deal Explained (2026)
excerpt: The Mix & Match deal is Domino's best everyday trick. Here's what qualifies, how to build the smartest order, and where people leave money behind.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Several Domino's items arranged for a Mix and Match order

faqs.question: How many items do you have to order for Mix & Match?
faqs.answer: You choose two or more qualifying items at the fixed per-item price. There is no requirement to pick the same item twice — you can mix a pizza with a side, for example.

faqs.question: Do specialty pizzas count in Mix & Match?
faqs.answer: Yes, most medium specialty pizzas qualify, though some premium pies may carry a small upcharge. The app shows eligibility as you build your order.

faqs.question: Is Mix & Match available for delivery?
faqs.answer: Yes, but delivery adds a fee. For the lowest total, choose carryout.

faqs.question: What items qualify for Mix & Match?
faqs.answer: Typically medium two-topping pizzas, most medium specialty pizzas, Stuffed Cheesy Bread, bread twists, oven-baked pasta, boneless chicken, and often salads and desserts. The app shows eligibility live as you build the order.

faqs.question: Is Mix & Match cheaper than ordering full price?
faqs.answer: Almost always, especially if you order a specialty pizza, since it costs the same per-item rate as a plain one. You get more food or more toppings for less.

faqs.question: Mix & Match or $6.99 Each — which is better?
faqs.answer: Mix & Match starts at two items; $6.99 Each needs three or more. For small orders use Mix & Match; for families or parties, compare both at checkout since the three-item deal often wins.

faqs.question: Can I add drinks to a Mix & Match order?
faqs.answer: Sometimes drinks qualify as an item, but availability varies by store. A 2-liter is cheap either way and a smart add for any group order.

content:
What Mix & Match Really Is

Think of Mix & Match as Domino's leaning over the counter and saying, pick a few things, we'll charge you a flat rate for each, stop overthinking it. That's basically the whole pitch. You choose two or more qualifying items, and every one lands at the same fixed price. No coupon to remember, no code to fumble at checkout, no fine print to squint at under your phone light. It just works, and that simplicity is half the reason it's outlasted nearly every other deal Domino's has ever run.

What I love about it — and I order a genuinely embarrassing amount of pizza, so trust me here — is the flexibility. You're not forced to buy two of the same thing the way some deals sneakily require. Grab a pizza and a side. Grab three totally different items. Get a pizza for you and pasta for your partner who's suddenly 'not in a pizza mood' tonight. The deal honestly doesn't care what you mix, and that freedom is exactly why it beats the fussier, more rigid promos out there.

Now, the exact per-item price moves around a bit over time and from store to store, because every Domino's is franchised and priced on its own. For years it's hovered in the same rough neighborhood, and the app always shows you the live number before you pay. Treat any figure in this guide as a realistic example, then let checkout confirm the real total. Deal? Good. Let's get into the useful stuff.

What Actually Qualifies

The eligible list is refreshingly generous, which is the best part of the whole thing. Medium two-topping pizzas, Stuffed Cheesy Bread, bread twists, oven-baked pasta, boneless chicken, and quite often salads and desserts too. But here's the kicker most people walk straight past: the medium specialty pizzas usually count. So a fully loaded ExtravaganZZa can cost you the same per-item price as a plain cheese. Read that twice. Why on earth would you order plain, then? Load it up. That's free flavor sitting right there on the table.

Here's a quick map of what typically plays and what doesn't, so you can build a cart in your head before you even open the app.

CategoryUsually Qualifies?Notes
Medium 2-topping pizzaYesThe classic building block of the deal
Medium specialty pizzaYesA few premium pies may add a small upcharge
Stuffed Cheesy Bread & bread twistsYesGreat low-cost filler for the table
Oven-baked pastaYesPerfect for the non-pizza eater
Boneless chicken & wingsUsuallyAdds protein without breaking the deal
Desserts & saladsOftenVaries by store and current promo
Large or XL pizzasNoMix & Match is built around the medium
DrinksSometimesCheck the app; a 2-liter is cheap regardless

The One Small Catch

A handful of premium or ultra-loaded specialty pizzas may carry a tiny upcharge, and some stores quietly tweak what's eligible. It's not a big deal, and you'll never get ambushed by it, because the app tells you exactly what qualifies as you build the order. The running total updates live with every item you add. So there's no guessing and no ugly surprise at the end. Watch that number climb, and you'll always know precisely where you stand before you commit.

Ordering for One (Yes, It Still Works)

People assume Mix & Match is a family-only deal. It isn't, and that myth costs solo diners money. Eating alone doesn't lock you out even slightly. Pair a medium two-topping with an order of boneless chicken or some cheesy bread, and you've got a proper dinner tonight plus a guaranteed lunch tomorrow. Since the price is fixed per item, leaning toward a specialty pizza just gets you more going on for the exact same cash. And honestly? Cold leftover specialty pizza at noon the next day is one of life's genuinely small, reliable joys. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

A Sample Solo Cart

Picture this order: one medium specialty pizza, one order of boneless chicken. Two items, both at the deal rate, and you're eating twice off it. That's a dinner and a lunch for the price most places charge for a single sad combo meal. Add a 20 oz drink if you want to round it out.

Ordering for the Whole Table

Feeding a family? This is where the deal really earns its keep and stops being clever and starts being essential. Two medium pizzas — say one pepperoni and one plain cheese for the picky kid who refuses anything with 'bits' on it — plus a shareable side and a dessert covers every mouth at the table without drama. I laid out several ready-to-tap combos in the family picks guide so you don't have to reinvent the wheel every Friday night. Toss in a 2-liter and nobody's asking for anything else for the rest of the evening.

The Three-Pizza Sweet Spot

Once you're ordering for four or more, three or four items becomes the natural size, and that's exactly when you should compare Mix & Match against the $6.99 Each deal, which I'll break down in a second. Bigger orders unlock better per-item math, so a full family order is genuinely one of the cheapest ways to eat per person at Domino's.

Mix & Match or $6.99 Each? Let's Settle It

Good question, and the honest answer depends entirely on how hungry your group is. Both are per-item deals, but they trigger at different thresholds, and knowing which to reach for saves real money.

DealMinimum ItemsBest ForWatch Out For
Mix & Match2 or moreSolo diners, couples, small ordersLarger orders may beat it
$6.99 Each3 or moreFamilies, parties, group ordersNeeds three items to trigger
50% Off Menu PizzasMenu-price pizzasA single specialty not in the dealLimited-time, comes and goes

My rule is dead simple. Build the cart, then glance at both totals right there at checkout and take whichever's lower. It takes thirty seconds and it routinely shaves a few bucks off. For a full rundown of every current offer, our coupons page keeps the live list.

Which Items Give You the Most Value?

Let's be strategic, because not every qualifying item is equal value inside the deal. Since the price per item is fixed, you want to fill your slots with the things that would normally cost the most on their own. That means specialty pizzas over plain ones, and Stuffed Cheesy Bread over a basic bread twist. The pepperoni is a safe crowd-pleaser, but if the deal lets you swap to a loaded specialty for the same money, take it every time. You're essentially getting the premium toppings thrown in for nothing.

How to Actually Order It, Step by Step

There's no secret handshake here, which is part of the charm. Open the Domino's app or website, head to the deals or Mix & Match section, and start adding qualifying items to your cart. The deal price applies automatically as you hit the item minimum — no code to paste, no hoops. If it isn't showing up, back out and double-check your items actually qualify, because that's almost always the reason. Pick carryout if you can, and make sure you're signed into your rewards account before you pay.

Getting the Rock-Bottom Total

Want the absolute cheapest version of any Mix & Match order? Stack three habits and don't skip any of them. Order through Mix & Match, choose carryout to dodge the delivery fee entirely, and stay signed into Domino's Rewards so the order still quietly banks points toward a free pizza down the line. That's a deal, a saved fee, and future free food all bundled into one order. Do that consistently and the savings pile up faster than you'd expect over a month or two. My complete method lives in the money-saving playbook if you want the whole system.

The Mistakes People Make

Two big ones, and I see them constantly. First, ordering plain items when a specialty qualifies for the same price — that's just leaving flavor on the counter for no reason. Second, defaulting to delivery out of habit when carryout would've saved the fee entirely. Neither mistake is dramatic on its own, but together they quietly inflate order after order. Now that you know, you won't make them.

Is It the Cheapest Deal Available?

Not always, and it depends entirely on how many items you are buying. Mix & Match is built around two items; a three-item offer beats it once you genuinely want three, and a single pizza is usually cheaper on the carryout special. We ran the arithmetic across every scenario in which Domino's deal is actually cheapest, including the trap where adding a third item to unlock a lower per-item price leaves you paying more overall.

The Bottom Line

Mix & Match is the deal I'd teach a total Domino's newcomer first, before anything else. It's flexible, it's simple, it covers solo dinners and family feasts alike, and it stacks beautifully with carryout and rewards. The exact per-item price shifts now and then and varies store to store, so let the checkout screen have the final word every time. We're an independent, unofficial guide here — Domino's writes the real rules. But of all the rules they've written, this deal is easily the best one.

faqs.question: Which is cheaper, Domino's or Pizza Hut?
faqs.answer: On the 2026 NetCredit US Pizza Index, which priced a medium cheese pizza through Grubhub and DoorDash across 180 cities, Pizza Hut averaged about $19.00 and Domino's about $19.33 — close enough that your local stores matter more than the national average. Ordering direct rather than through a delivery app changes both numbers far more than the gap between them.

faqs.question: Which is cheaper, Domino's or Papa John's?
faqs.answer: On that same 2026 index Papa John's was the cheapest of the big three at roughly $16.65 for a medium cheese, against Domino's at $19.33. But the index measures third-party delivery app pricing on one specific pizza — on a large pizza bought direct on carryout inside a deal, Domino's is usually competitive or ahead.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest pizza chain overall?
faqs.answer: Little Caesars, and it is not close. The 2026 index put its medium cheese at around $10.27, roughly 46% below Domino's. Papa Murphy's (about $12.38, sold unbaked to finish at home) and MOD Pizza (about $12.45) came next. If price is the only thing that matters, none of the big three is your answer.

faqs.question: Why do price comparisons disagree with each other?
faqs.answer: Because they measure different things. A study priced through Grubhub or DoorDash captures marked-up menus plus platform fees; a like-for-like carryout comparison bought direct gives completely different numbers, often several dollars lower. Neither is wrong — they are answering different questions, and the ranking can flip between them.

faqs.question: Which pizza chain has the best rewards programme?
faqs.answer: It depends on how you order rather than which is objectively better. Domino's rewards you per qualifying order, so frequent smaller orders reach a free pizza faster. Pizza Hut and Papa John's reward per dollar spent, which favours larger baskets. A student ordering a small pizza most weeks does better at Domino's; a family placing big orders occasionally does better on a per-dollar scheme.

faqs.question: Which chain is best for a large group?
faqs.answer: Compare the multi-item bundle rather than a single pizza. Domino's Mix & Match style pricing and Pizza Hut's dinner box formats are both designed for this, and the effective per-person cost is usually much lower than any single-pizza comparison suggests. Price the actual basket you intend to buy at each, in the same channel, on the same night.

faqs.question: Who invented stuffed crust?
faqs.answer: Pizza Hut, back in 1995, and it remains the item most associated with the brand. Domino's only launched its own version, Parmesan Stuffed Crust, in 2025 — which is why the comparison on that particular item is newer than most people assume.

faqs.question: Is Papa John's actually better quality?
faqs.answer: That is a taste question rather than a factual one, and the brand's long-running "Better Ingredients" positioning is marketing rather than an independent finding. What is objectively different is that Papa John's includes a garlic dipping sauce with pizzas, which most people either specifically want or do not care about at all.

faqs.question: Does ordering direct really cost less than a delivery app?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, and often by more than people expect. Third-party platforms commonly show higher menu prices than the chain's own app, then add service and delivery fees on top. If you are comparing chains, comparing them on the same channel is the only way to get an answer that means anything.

faqs.question: So which should I order from?
faqs.answer: Cheapest possible pizza: Little Caesars. Cheapest of the big three on a single medium through an app: Papa John's. Best value on a large carryout order inside a deal: usually Domino's. Best if you want pan or stuffed crust specifically: Pizza Hut. The honest answer is that the winner changes with the order, which is why a single ranking is not very useful.

content:
The Short Answer

There isn't one winner, and any article that gives you a single ranking is hiding the interesting part. The cheapest chain changes depending on what you order and how you order it, and the gap between those two things is bigger than the gap between the brands.

Here is the summary before the detail:

  • Cheapest pizza of all: Little Caesars, by a wide margin — and none of the big three is close
  • Cheapest of the big three on a single medium cheese through a delivery app: Papa John's
  • Best value on a large order bought direct on carryout: usually Domino's
  • Best if you specifically want pan or stuffed crust: Pizza Hut

One thing to know about this page before you read on: this is an independent guide, not run by any of these three chains. That is precisely why it can tell you a competitor is cheaper on a given order — none of them would ever publish that.

What the 2026 Price Data Actually Says

The most useful recent dataset is NetCredit's 2026 US Pizza Index, which priced a medium cheese pizza from the ten biggest US chains through Grubhub and DoorDash across 180 cities. Using one identical item across a lot of places is the only way to compare fairly, so it is a genuinely good methodology — as long as you understand what it measured.

ChainAverage medium cheesevs Domino's
Little Caesars~$10.27About 46% cheaper
Papa Murphy's~$12.38Much cheaper (sold unbaked)
MOD Pizza~$12.45Much cheaper
Papa John's~$16.65Cheaper
Pizza Hut~$19.00Slightly cheaper
Domino's~$19.33—

Two things jump out. Papa John's beat both of the other big-three chains on this measure, which surprises people who assume Domino's is the budget option. And the difference between Pizza Hut and Domino's — about 33 cents — is small enough that it is noise. Your two local stores will differ by more than that, because every one of these chains is franchised and sets its own prices.

The Catch Everyone Skips

Here is the part that changes the whole conclusion, and most comparison articles leave it out.

That index priced pizzas through Grubhub and DoorDash. Third-party delivery platforms routinely carry higher menu prices than the chain's own app, and then add service and delivery fees on top. So the index is an accurate answer to the question "what does a medium cheese cost through a delivery app" — which is not the same question as "which chain is cheapest".

Look at what happens to one chain across channels:

Same chain, different routeExample price
Domino's medium cheese via delivery app~$19.33
Domino's large one-topping, direct carryout~$13.99

That is a bigger pizza for around five dollars less, from the same chain, on the same day. The channel you order through matters more than the brand you order from. If you take one thing from this page, take that.

It also means any comparison is only valid if you price the chains the same way: same size, same toppings, same channel, same night. Our carryout deals guide works through what that gap is worth on a normal order.

How Each Chain Structures Its Value

The three brands are not trying to win on the same thing, which is why single-item comparisons are misleading.

Domino's builds around multi-item deals. Its Mix & Match style pricing is designed so that adding a second or third item drops the per-item price, which means a single pizza is close to its worst-value order. Buy the way the deal wants you to buy and the maths improves sharply — see our Mix & Match explainer.

Pizza Hut leans on bundles and formats. Dinner-box style packages that combine pizza, sides and dessert at a set price are the brand's traditional strength, and they suit a family table better than they suit one person.

Papa John's tends to compete on the headline price of the pizza itself, which is consistent with it winning the single-medium comparison above. It also includes a garlic dipping sauce with pizzas as standard, which is a small thing that a lot of its customers are specifically loyal to.

The practical consequence: compare the basket you actually intend to buy, not one pizza. A group order and a solo order can rank these three chains in different orders.

Rewards: The Structural Difference

All three run a loyalty scheme, and the marketing makes them sound similar. The mechanics are not.

ChainHow you earnWho it suits
Domino'sPoints per qualifying orderFrequent, smaller orders
Pizza HutPoints per dollar spentLarger baskets
Papa John'sPoints per dollar spentLarger baskets

This is the difference that actually matters. Domino's rewards you for ordering often; the other two reward you for spending more.

So a student who orders a small pizza most weeks accumulates toward a free one fastest at Domino's, because a $12 order and a $40 order earn the same. A family that places a large order once a month does better on a per-dollar scheme, where that $60 basket earns sixty times what a single dollar does.

Neither is generous, and none of them should decide where you order from tonight. But if you consistently use one chain, picking the scheme that matches your ordering pattern is worth a free pizza or two a year. Our Domino's Rewards guide covers the thresholds on that side in detail.

What Each One Is Genuinely Best At

Away from price, the three do have real differences.

Pizza Hut owns pan and stuffed crust. It invented stuffed crust in 1995 and its Original Pan pizza is the item most people associate with the brand. If a thick, rich, pan-baked pizza is what you actually want, that is Pizza Hut's home ground — Domino's Handmade Pan is the nearest equivalent on its menu but it is not the brand's defining product.

Domino's is the delivery and ordering operation. The tracking, the app, the speed of the whole process and the breadth of deal structures are where the company has invested for years. It also now has its own stuffed crust — Parmesan Stuffed Crust launched in 2025, thirty years after Pizza Hut's, which is covered in our stuffed crust guide.

Papa John's competes on the pizza itself. The long-running "Better Ingredients, Better Pizza" line is marketing rather than an independent finding, and it is worth treating it that way. The garlic sauce included with every pizza is a genuine, concrete differentiator, and for a lot of its customers it is the whole reason they order there.

The Awkward Answer: Little Caesars

If your question is strictly "which chain is cheapest", none of the big three is the honest answer.

Little Caesars came in around $10.27 on the 2026 index — roughly 46% below Domino's for essentially the same item. The model is different: pizzas are made ready to collect rather than ordered and then made, which strips out both waiting and delivery.

What you give up is customisation, delivery in most cases, and the deal structures that make a big Domino's order work. But if the actual requirement is feeding people cheaply, pretending the big three compete on that would be dishonest. Papa Murphy's (around $12.38, sold unbaked for you to finish in your own oven) and MOD Pizza (around $12.45) sit in the same value bracket.

Which Should You Order? By Situation

  • Cheapest possible pizza, no other requirements: Little Caesars
  • One medium pizza delivered through an app: Papa John's, on the 2026 numbers
  • A large pizza plus sides, bought direct on carryout: usually Domino's, because the deal structure rewards multiple items
  • Pan or stuffed crust specifically: Pizza Hut
  • Feeding a family with mixed tastes: price the actual bundle at each — this is where the single-pizza rankings break down completely
  • You order pizza most weeks: Domino's rewards, because it pays per order rather than per dollar
  • You order rarely but large: Pizza Hut or Papa John's rewards

How to Compare Them Yourself Tonight

National averages are a starting point, not an answer, because all three chains are franchised and price locally. Ten minutes of checking beats any article, including this one:

  • Open all three apps, not the delivery platforms. Comparing a chain app against a Grubhub listing is not a comparison
  • Build the same basket in each — same size, roughly the same toppings, same sides
  • Set all three to carryout, then all three to delivery. The ranking genuinely can flip between the two
  • Read to the final total, after tax and fees. The menu price is the least useful number on the screen
  • Check the deals tab in each before you finish. A chain that looks expensive at menu price often is not once an offer is applied

The Honest Verdict

On the 2026 delivery-app data, Papa John's is the cheapest of the big three, Pizza Hut and Domino's are effectively tied behind it, and Little Caesars is far below all of them.

But that ranking describes one pizza bought one way. Order a large on carryout inside a deal and Domino's moves to the front; want a pan pizza and Pizza Hut was never really in a price contest. The chains have arranged themselves so that each one wins a different question, which is exactly why none of them will publish a comparison like this.

The genuinely useful takeaway is not a brand at all. It is that ordering direct rather than through a delivery app, and taking carryout rather than delivery, will save you more than switching chains ever will. That is true at all three, and it is worth more than any loyalty scheme.

content:
This Isn't a Worst-Items List

Almost everything on the Domino's menu is decent food at a fair price, and lists that pretend otherwise are usually written by someone who hasn't eaten there.

This is a narrower question: which specific choices cost more than they give back? Not bad items — bad trades. An upgrade you pay for and can't taste. A format that costs double per ounce. An item that's genuinely good but arrives ruined because of how you ordered it.

Every verdict below has the arithmetic behind it. Prices are examples, since franchised stores set their own — but the comparisons hold wherever you are.

1. A Medium When the Large Is Two Dollars More

The most common way to overpay at Domino's, and it happens because a medium feels like the sensible middle option.

SizeAreaExample priceCost per square inch
Small 10"~79 sq in~$8.99~11.4¢
Medium 12"~113 sq in~$10.99~9.7¢
Large 14"~154 sq in~$12.99~8.4¢

Stepping from medium to large is typically about two dollars for roughly 36% more pizza. Nothing else on the menu gives you that much more food for that little, and the gap widens as the pizza gets bigger because dough is the cheap part.

Order instead: the large, unless you genuinely can't eat it and won't keep leftovers. If you're worried about waste, box half before you sit down — cold pizza the next day is a better outcome than paying more per slice tonight. Our sizes guide has the full comparison.

2. Extra Cheese

The upgrade with the weakest return on the whole menu. Roughly $1.50 to $3.00 for about 40 extra calories a slice — around 320 across a large — on a pizza whose defining ingredient is already cheese.

The problem isn't that it does nothing. It's that the difference is small enough that most people wouldn't reliably pick the extra-cheese pizza out of two, while the price difference is the same as adding a whole topping that you would notice.

Order instead: a real topping for the same money. Or, if it's richness you're after, switch the crust — Handmade Pan changes the pizza far more than extra cheese does, and our crust guide covers what each one actually tastes like.

3. Individual Drink Bottles

On a per-ounce basis this is the worst value on the menu, and it isn't close.

OptionVolumePricePer ounce
20 oz bottle20 oz~$2.49~12.5¢
2-litre bottle67.6 oz~$3.49~5.2¢

Three bottles cost about $7.47 and contain less liquid than one 2-litre at about $3.49. There is no order size at which three bottles is the right call.

Order instead: the 2-litre, unless you're genuinely one person who wants exactly one drink. More on the whole range in our drinks guide.

4. Rebuilding a Specialty by Hand

People assume build-your-own is always cheaper. When you want a lot of toppings, it's the opposite.

Route to the same pizzaExample cost
Large base + 8 toppings at ~$2.50 each~$31.99
ExtravaganZZa from the specialty menu~$16.99

About fifteen dollars more to assemble the same pizza yourself. Per-topping charges compound fast, and the specialty menu exists precisely because Domino's prices those combinations as a bundle.

Order instead: build your own for two or three toppings, and take the specialty when you want a loaded pizza. Better still, start from a specialty and remove what you don't like — removals normally cost nothing, so an ExtravaganZZa without olives is the same price. The full lineup is in our specialty pizzas guide.

5. A Specialty Pizza at Menu Price

Having just recommended specialty pizzas, here's the caveat: don't buy one at menu price if you can avoid it.

A large specialty sits around $16.99 on the menu. The same pizza inside a live offer is frequently nearer $9.99, and a percentage-off promotion takes it to around $8.49. That's a seven-to-eight dollar spread on an identical pizza depending only on which screen you ordered from.

Order instead: check the deals tab before adding anything. We ran the full comparison in which Domino's deal is actually cheapest.

6. Loaded Tots and Lava Cakes on a Long Delivery

Neither of these is a bad item. Both are among the better things on the menu. The mistake is when you order them.

  • Loaded Tots exist to be crisp. Sealed in a bag with hot cheese on top, steam softens them, and twenty-five minutes later you have warm potato
  • Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes depend on a molten centre. It sets as they cool, and a cold lava cake is an ordinary chocolate cake

Order instead: both, on carryout, where they're excellent. On a long delivery, pick bread-based sides and the Cookie Brownie, which don't depend on temperature. Our sides guide covers which items travel and which don't.

7. Stuffed Cheesy Bread Treated as a Side

This one needs care, because the item is genuinely good and fairly priced. The mistake is the role you give it.

PriceCalories
Full order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread~$7.99~1,040
Large cheese pizza~$12.99~2,160

The "side" carries about half a pizza's calories at roughly 60% of a pizza's price. It isn't a side by any sensible definition — it's a second main course wearing a side's label.

Order instead: the same bread, but replacing two slices rather than accompanying them. Or Parmesan Bread Bites, which are around $4.99 for sixteen pieces and split far better around a table.

8. Creamy Dips, If You're Counting

Small item, and only relevant if calories matter to you — but then it matters more than people expect.

A ranch or blue cheese cup is around 170 calories against roughly 45 for marinara. Two or three cups across a shared order is a couple of hundred calories nobody logged, sitting quietly next to the pizza that everyone did.

Order instead: marinara, if you want a dip without thinking about it. Full numbers in our calories guide.

What Is Worth Ordering

A list of things to skip isn't much use without the other half, so:

  • Parmesan Bread Bites — around $4.99 for sixteen pieces, the best value per piece on the menu
  • The large over the medium — the price step up is usually a couple of dollars for meaningfully more pizza; see our sizes guide
  • Specialty pizzas inside a deal — eight toppings for the price of a two-topping build
  • An oven-baked sandwich for one person — similar money to a small pizza, no leftovers, travels better
  • The free customisations — swapping the sauce, going light on cheese, changing the crust. These cost nothing and change the pizza more than any paid upgrade does

That last point is the one worth remembering. The best-value changes on the Domino's menu are all free. A garlic Parmesan base instead of tomato transforms a pizza and costs zero; extra cheese costs three dollars and barely registers.

The Pattern

Look back at the eight and they're mostly one of three things:

  • Paying for volume in the wrong format — bottles instead of a 2-litre, toppings instead of a specialty
  • Paying for an upgrade you can't detect — extra cheese, the bread bowl
  • Ordering a good item at the wrong moment — tots and lava cakes on a long delivery, a specialty at menu price

None of it requires eating less or enjoying it less. It's the same meal, ordered slightly differently, for less money — which is the only kind of saving worth writing down.

content:
You're Probably Overpaying (Most People Are)

Domino's is already decent value on its own. But most folks walk right past the savings without noticing, ordering at full menu price like it's the only option on the table. It isn't. Not even close. Before we get into the how, do this: play the calculator at the top of this page. Pick your order type, drag that subtotal slider, flip the rewards toggle, and watch the number drop in real time. Seeing your own order shrink is more convincing than anything I can write. Then come back and I'll walk you through the nine moves behind that drop, roughly in order of how much each one matters.

The Nine Tactics, Ranked by Impact

If you're in a hurry, here's the whole playbook in one table. The details are below, but this is the shape of it.

TacticTypical SavingEffort
Order inside a deal15–25%None
Choose carryout$4–6 + tipA short drive
Order in the appUnlocks best pricingNone
Use rewardsA free pizza over timeNone
Size up smartlyBetter cost per sliceNone
Split a big orderCrushes per-person costA little planning

1. Start With a Deal, Always

This is the big one, so I'm putting it first. Never add an item at full price if a deal already covers it. Mix & Match and $6.99 Each wrap up most of what you'd order anyway — pizzas, sides, pasta, chicken. So build your entire order inside one of them from the very first click, not as an afterthought at the end. Ordering full-price and hoping to fix it later is exactly how people end up paying twenty percent too much without ever realizing it happened.

2. Go Get It Yourself

Delivery tacks on a fee, usually four to six bucks, before you've even thought about a tip. That's real money on a small order — sometimes a third of the whole bill. If picking up is even remotely convenient, carryout wins, full stop. The short version fits on a bumper sticker: your car is cheaper than their driver. And carryout-only specials, which you'll find on the coupons page, often sweeten the deal even further beyond just skipping the fee.

3. Order Through the App

Phone orders quietly miss the best pricing, and a surprising number of people still don't know this. The app and website reflect the current national promotions and unlock carryout-only specials you literally cannot get by calling the store. It's a couple of taps for a genuine discount. If you're still dialing the number out of habit, you're leaving money on the counter every single time.

4. Join Rewards — It's Free

Every qualifying order quietly banks points toward a free pizza, and signing up costs you absolutely nothing. There's no annual fee, no catch, no reason on earth not to. Over a few months of normal ordering, that's a free pie you'd otherwise have paid full price for. The full breakdown's in the rewards explainer, but the summary is simple — be signed in every time so no order goes uncounted.

5. Size Up on Purpose

Here's a bit of pizza economics people consistently miss. The gap between a medium and a large is often just a dollar or two, but you get a lot more pizza for that dollar. Measured per slice, the large is usually the smartest buy on the whole board, and the sizes guide proves it with the numbers. Don't be shy about sizing up, especially when you're feeding more than one person — the leftovers alone justify it.

6. Sneak a Specialty Into the Deal

Since specialty pizzas usually qualify for Mix & Match at the same per-item price as a basic pie, ordering one is basically getting a pile of premium toppings for free. Plain cheese and a fully loaded specialty can cost the exact same inside the deal. So take the specialty every time. Your taste buds win and your wallet doesn't notice the difference. There's genuinely no downside here.

7. Cut the Stuff You Won't Finish

Extra dips, premium toppings, that second dessert nobody actually asked for — it all quietly creeps onto the total while you're not looking. The app is very, very good at nudging you toward add-ons. Order what you'll genuinely eat, not what looks tempting on the screen at 9pm when everything sounds like a great idea. Be a little ruthless in the cart and you'll thank yourself at checkout.

8. Watch for the Wild Cards

Limited-time promos like Emergency Pizza or a 50%-off-menu week can occasionally beat the standing deals by a wide margin. Peek at the deals tab before you commit — it takes five seconds and every so often it saves you ten dollars flat. The wild cards are unpredictable, which is exactly why checking becomes a reflex worth building into every order.

9. Split a Big Order

The $6.99 Each deal rewards bulk, so pooling an order with roommates, coworkers or family absolutely crushes the per-person cost. Everyone throws in a few bucks, you hit the three-item threshold easily, and suddenly dinner costs everyone less than a sad fast-food combo. Pizza's always been cheaper by the crowd — that's kind of its whole thing, and it's a lever most people forget they have.

A Real Example: Watch the Total Drop

Talk is cheap, so let's run actual numbers. Picture the same food ordered two ways — the careless way and the smart way.

OrderFull-Price WaySmart Way
2 large pizzas~$26.00Deal pricing
Cheesy bread + dessert~$13.00Deal pricing
Delivery fee + tip~$10.00$0 (carryout)
Rewards points earnedNone (guest)Toward free pizza
Rough total~$49~$32

Same food. Roughly seventeen dollars saved, plus points banking for later. That's not a magic trick — it's just deal, carryout, and rewards working together.

Stack It All Together

None of these tricks is dramatic on its own. The real magic is in doing them all at once. A deal, plus carryout, plus app ordering, plus rewards — layer all four and a normal family order can slide 25 to 40 percent below full price, as that example just showed. That's not a wild claim, it's plain arithmetic. Numbers move around by location, so let checkout confirm the final total, and keep the menu with prices handy when you plan. And yes, this is an independent, unofficial guide, written by people who genuinely can't stand watching someone overpay for a pizza when two minutes of planning would've fixed it.

content:
Is It Even Worth It? Short Answer: Yeah.

Loyalty programs can be a real hassle — endless tiers, points that vanish the moment you forget about them, apps that nag you every other day with notifications you didn't ask for. So I completely understand the skepticism. But Domino's Rewards, the one half of us still call Piece of the Pie out of pure habit, is refreshingly simple by comparison. You order, you earn, you eventually get free food. That's the entire loop, start to finish. If you buy Domino's even once a month, joining is a genuine no-brainer, because it costs you nothing and quietly discounts a future order while you're not even paying attention.

This guide walks through exactly how it works, what you earn, what you can cash in for, whether it's actually worth your time, and the small habits that squeeze the most out of it. No fluff. Let's get into it.

How to Sign Up (It Takes Two Minutes)

There's almost nothing to it, which is the point. Create a free account in the Domino's app or on the website, and you're enrolled in rewards from your very next qualifying order. No membership fee, no card to carry, no commitment. If you already order Domino's without an account, you've literally been leaving free pizza on the table this whole time. Fix that today and your future self will thank you in about six orders.

How the Points Add Up

The classic setup hands you 10 points for every qualifying order of five dollars or more, calculated before tax and tip. And here's a detail people really appreciate — it doesn't matter one bit whether you're getting delivery or carryout. Points are points either way. Domino's has also tested newer tiered versions that let you cash in smaller point totals for smaller items, so the genuinely smart move is to glance at the current catalogue in the app before you assume the old rules still apply. These programs evolve, and this one has changed shape more than once over the years.

What You DoWhat You Earn
Qualifying order of $5+ (before tax/tip)10 points
Delivery or carryoutSame points either way
Ordering through a deal like Mix & MatchStill earns full points
Signing up / occasional bonus promosExtra points, varies

Do Points Expire?

They can, and this trips a lot of people up. Points generally lapse after a stretch of account inactivity, so if you order Domino's a few times a year you're perfectly fine, but if you go completely dormant for ages, don't be shocked to find your balance reset to zero one day. The fix couldn't be simpler — just placing a qualifying order keeps the whole thing alive and ticking. Use it or slowly lose it, basically. It's not aggressive about it, but it's worth knowing.

The Free Pizza Math

Let's talk about the payoff, because that's really why you're here. Under the traditional program, 60 points gets you a free medium two-topping pizza. That's roughly six qualifying orders — not instant gratification, sure, but honestly not a marathon either. Order weekly and you're eating free within about a month and a half. Some of the newer options let you trade as few as 20 points for a side or a dessert, which is a genuinely nice touch when you don't feel like holding out for the full pie. Want a lava cake right now instead of a pizza in six weeks? That flexibility is welcome.

Example RewardPoints (approx.)Roughly How Many Orders
Bread twists or a drink20 points~2 orders
Stuffed Cheesy Bread or pasta40 points~4 orders
Free medium 2-topping pizza60 points~6 orders

These tiers are examples — the live, current versions are laid out on our rewards page, and the app always shows the real numbers. Point being, you've got choices about how patient you want to be.

Is It Actually Worth It? Let's Do Real Numbers

Here's the honest math. If a free medium two-topping is worth roughly ten bucks and it takes about six qualifying orders to earn, you're effectively getting a small discount baked into every single order without lifting a finger. Compare that to the loyalty programs at some other chains, which pile on confusing tiers and expiration traps, and Domino's simplicity starts to look like a feature rather than a limitation. It won't make you rich. But free pizza every couple of months for doing something you were already going to do? That's a quiet, easy win.

Getting the Most Out of It

Here's a thing worth knowing that saves you from a pointless mistake. Points come per order, not per dollar spent. So splitting one giant order into a bunch of tiny ones to farm extra points is way more hassle than it's worth, and frankly a little silly. Don't bother. The only habit that actually matters is making sure you're signed in every single time, so no order ever slips through uncounted. That's genuinely it. Then pair rewards with a value deal and carryout, and now you're stacking savings on top of savings on top of a slow drip toward free food.

The One Habit That Matters Most

Log in before you order. Every time. That's the whole trick. People lose out not because the program is stingy but because they check out as a guest and forget. Make signing in the first thing you do, and the points take care of themselves.

Rewards and Deals Play Nice Together

This is the part that quietly makes the whole thing worth it. You still earn points when you order through Mix & Match or a carryout special — the deal discount and the points aren't mutually exclusive, which surprises people. So over a few months of totally normal ordering, you're pocketing a free pizza on top of the discounts you were already getting anyway. It's not flashy. There's no confetti when it happens. It just works, steadily, in the background, and one day you open the app and realize there's a free pie sitting there waiting for you. The whole cost-cutting picture fits together in the money-saving guide, and it pairs perfectly with the offers on our coupons page.

The Fine Print, Because There's Always Fine Print

Point values, redemption tiers and qualifying minimums are all set by Domino's, and they shift from time to time without much fanfare or warning. We're an independent, unofficial guide, so before you go counting on a specific reward at checkout, double-check the current terms in the official app. Nobody likes getting to that final screen expecting a free pizza that quietly isn't there anymore. Verify first, then enjoy the win. And if you order Domino's with any regularity at all, that win is coming sooner than you think.

Four sizes, a couple of crust exceptions, and prices that jump in ways that don't always feel logical. No wonder people stand there in the app second-guessing themselves. Should you go big and risk waste, or play it safe and end up raiding the fridge an hour later? Domino's Pizza Sizes at a Glance

Before we go one by one, here's the whole lineup in a single view. Keep this in your back pocket and you'll never fumble a pizza order again.

Small — 10 Inches

The little one. Ten inches across, cut into six slices, and perfectly sized for a single person who isn't trying to eat pizza for breakfast the next morning. It's a tidy solo dinner without the guilt of a box full of leftovers staring at you from the fridge. There's a bonus reason to know the small, too — it's the only size you can get on the Gluten Free crust. So if wheat's off your list, this is your default whether you like it or not. Just know that Domino's makes it in a shared kitchen, so it isn't suited to severe allergies or celiac. Worth flagging if that's you.

Medium — 12 Inches

Twelve inches, eight slices. Enough for one genuinely hungry person, or two people who are treating pizza as a snack rather than the main event. But here's the fact worth tucking away: the medium two-topping is the classic Mix & Match building block, which is precisely why this size shows up in so many deals. If you're ordering to a promotion, medium is often the size that unlocks the best pricing. When in doubt, medium plays nicely with just about every offer Domino's runs.

Large — 14 Inches (The One I'd Order)

Fourteen inches, eight slices, and almost always the best bang for your buck on the entire menu. I'll be blunt — this is the size I default to nine times out of ten. The price bump from medium to large is usually just a couple of dollars, but you get noticeably more pizza for it. Here's why: a pizza's area grows with the square of its radius, so a 14-inch large actually holds a lot more pizza than a 12-inch medium, not just a little more. Do the per-slice math and the large quietly wins nearly every time. Feeding two or more people? Start here and stop overthinking it.

The Per-Slice Value Truth

People obsess over the sticker price and miss the real question, which is cost per slice, or better yet, cost per square inch of actual pizza. When you measure it that way, the medium-to-large jump is one of the best value moves in fast food. You're paying a small premium for a big chunk more food. A large pepperoni through a deal is, pound for pound, hard to beat.

Extra Large — 16 Inches

This one's a bit of a specialist, and I mean that as a compliment. Sixteen inches, available on Brooklyn Style crust only, cut into six big, thin, foldable New-York-style slices. It's the most pizza Domino's will hand you in a single pie, and those foldable slices are honestly just fun to eat — there's something deeply satisfying about folding a slice in half, street-vendor style. If you're chasing that classic pizzeria vibe rather than maximum topping thickness, the Extra Large is your pick. Just remember it's Brooklyn crust only, so if you're a deep-dish-at-heart person, this isn't your lane.

How Many Pizzas Do You Actually Need?

This is the question that really matters when you're ordering for a group, and guessing wrong means either hungry guests or a fridge full of sad leftovers. Here's my rough planning table. It assumes normal appetites, so bump it up for teenagers or a football crowd.

PeopleSuggested OrderWhy
11 Small or MediumA full meal with little or no waste
21 LargeBest value, likely a slice or two left over
3–42 LargeBeats one XL on both quantity and price
5–63 Large (use $6.99 Each)Bulk deals kick in and crush the per-person cost
7+4+ Large or a party orderSee the family and catering approach

So Which One Do You Actually Order?

Let me make this dead simple. Eating solo? A small or medium is plenty — lean small if you truly don't want leftovers. Just the two of you? Large, easy call, don't second-guess it. Three or more mouths at the table? Here's the move most people get wrong: skip the single Extra Large and grab two larges through a value deal instead. You'll come out ahead on both total quantity and price, and everyone gets more topping choice. For a full family game plan, the family picks guide maps it all out combo by combo.

Don't Forget the Crust

Size is only half the decision — crust matters just as much, sometimes more. Hand Tossed is the pillowy default, Handmade Pan the indulgent one, Crunchy Thin for the anti-bread crowd, and Brooklyn Style for those big foldable slices. Not every crust comes in every size, either. You'll find the full crust and size pairings on the menu and prices page before you lock in your order.

A Trick for Kids and Parties

Slice counts are standard out of the oven, but you're not stuck with them. You can ask the store to cut a large into ten or twelve smaller pieces at no extra charge, which is a genuine lifesaver at kids' parties where tiny hands and giant slices don't mix. Little request, big difference when there's a crowd of small humans involved.

A Quick Word on Calories

Bigger pizza, more calories — no surprise there. But the slice size matters as much as the count. A large slice packs more than a small one, so 'just one slice' isn't the same across sizes. If you're watching intake, ordering a smaller size and pairing it with a zero-sugar drink is an easy lever, as is choosing Crunchy Thin crust, which trims some of the dough. For the exact per-slice numbers by size and crust, see our Domino's calories and nutrition guide.

One Last Thing

Prices bounce around by location — a large in a big city might run a couple dollars more than the same pie in a small town, and that's just how franchising works. Since this is an independent, unofficial guide, the official Domino's app always has the final say on what you'll actually pay. Use this to plan the right size and the right number of pizzas, then let checkout confirm the number. Order smart, and nobody leaves the table hungry or overcharged. That's the whole goal.

content:
Ordering for a Family Is Basically Diplomacy

Anyone who's fed a table of kids and grown-ups at once knows the drill. One won't touch a vegetable. One wants everything on it, extra everything. Someone's suddenly decided this week that they don't like cheese, which, at a pizza dinner, is a genuinely bold stance to take. The trick isn't hunting for one magical pizza that pleases everybody — that pizza doesn't exist and never has. The real trick is covering all the bases without blowing the budget or losing your mind. Try the interactive picks at the top of the page for ready-to-tap combos, then stick around for the reasoning, the bundles, and a few tricks for the tricky eaters. Prices here are examples, so double-check at checkout as always.

The Safe Bets for Kids

Start with the reliable stuff. A classic pepperoni or a plain cheese on Hand Tossed crust is your foundation, full stop. These are the pizzas that vanish without a single complaint, and ordered through a value deal they barely dent the total. Don't underestimate boring, either — boring feeds children reliably, night after night, and on a chaotic weeknight that reliability is worth its weight in gold. Got a really picky one? Ask for light cheese or just a light sprinkle of pepperoni so it still feels like 'their' pizza with zero surprises to negotiate over.

Something for the Grown-Ups

Now give the adults something with a little ambition, because they deserve a real dinner too, not just the crusts the kids abandoned. A Large pepperoni sitting next to the fully loaded ExtravaganZZa covers both the plain crowd and the folks who actually want some flavor happening on their slice. And if your household skips pork for any reason, the Philly Cheese Steak is a genuinely great shout — no pork, all savory, and it feels a bit special without costing a cent extra inside a deal. Mixing one 'safe' pizza with one 'interesting' pizza is the single most reliable family formula I know, and I've tested it more times than I can count.

Handling Allergies and Dietary Needs

Every family has its constraints, and pizza night shouldn't leave anyone out. If someone's vegetarian, the Pacific Veggie is a proper pizza in its own right, not a sad afterthought — the full specialty pizza lineup is worth a look. Avoiding pork? The Philly Cheese Steak and plenty of chicken options have you covered. Gluten a concern? There's a Small Gluten Free crust, though it's made in a shared kitchen, so it suits a preference more than a serious medical allergy. The point is, you can almost always build an order where every single person at the table has something they're genuinely happy to eat. That's the goal.

Sides Do the Heavy Lifting

Here's where a lot of family orders quietly fall short — they stop at pizza. Don't. Stuffed Cheesy Bread and boneless chicken stretch the meal further and, crucially, give the kid who's 'not in a pizza mood' an actual escape hatch. There's always one, every single time. And a 2-liter is by far the cheapest way to keep everyone's cup full without buying six separate bottles that cost more and create a pile of trash. Little decisions, but they add up to a smoother, cheaper, less argumentative dinner.

Ready-Made Family Bundles

You don't have to build this from scratch every time. Here are the go-to bundles I reach for, sized by crowd. Adjust for appetites — a table of teenagers eats like a table of adults and then some.

CrowdThe OrderRough Deal Route
Family of 32 medium pizzas + cheesy breadMix & Match
Family of 42 large pizzas + 1 side + 2-literMix & Match, carryout
Family of 5–63 pizzas + boneless chicken + dessert$6.99 Each
Birthday / party4+ pizzas + multiple sides + drinks$6.99 Each or party order

The Cheat-Sheet Rule of Thumb

Let me hand you the formula I actually lean on so you never have to guess again. Two large pizzas, one shareable side, one 2-liter comfortably feeds a family of four with leftovers waiting for tomorrow's lunch. That's your baseline, memorize it. Order the whole thing through Mix & Match and grab it carryout, and you've fed the entire crew for a very reasonable number — the kind that doesn't make you wince when you tap pay. Bigger family? Add a third pizza and lean on the $6.99 Each deal instead. The interactive picks tool up top gives you a few tuned-up versions depending on the size and mood of your crew.

Feeding a Birthday Party or Big Group

When the crowd gets past six, the rules shift a little. Order more variety, not just more of the same, because a room full of kids will have wildly different opinions and you want easy wins. A stack of pepperoni and cheese covers the safe crowd, one or two specialties keep the adults happy, and a couple of shareable sides fill the gaps. Lean hard on the $6.99 Each deal here — it's built for exactly this kind of bulk order, and it keeps the per-head cost genuinely low. Order ahead of time if you can, especially on a busy weekend evening, so a big order doesn't leave you waiting while hungry kids stage a small revolt.

Squeezing the Price Down

The money-saving rules are the same as always, they just matter far more when you're buying for a whole table. Choose carryout to kill the delivery fee, order in the app to catch the best pricing and browse the current deals, and stay logged into Domino's Rewards so even the big family order banks points toward a free pizza down the line. Family orders are large, which means they earn and save more than a solo order ever could — so use that scale to your advantage instead of letting it work against you. The full method's laid out in the money-saving playbook.

The Bottom Line

Feeding a family at Domino's isn't about finding one perfect pizza. It's about mixing safe and interesting, propping the meal up with a couple of smart sides, and running the whole thing through a deal so the total stays friendly. Do that, and you get the rare weeknight miracle: a table where everyone's actually eating and nobody's complaining. We're an independent, unofficial guide, so let the official app confirm the real prices and deals before you pay. Then go enjoy the quiet, and maybe grab a slice for yourself before it's gone.

content:
Why Everyone Searches This

Domino's basically built its entire reputation on delivery — fast, trackable, dependable, the pizza that actually shows up when it says it will. So when the craving hits at 8pm and you type 'Domino's delivery near me' into your phone, you're in very good company. Millions of people do the exact same thing every single day. Let's cut through the noise and cover what actually matters: finding the right store, knowing how long you'll really wait, understanding that fee, tipping the right way, tracking your order, and spending as little as humanly possible getting a hot pizza to your front door. Everything you need, in one place.

First, Find Your Store

Delivery gets handled by whichever franchise store covers your specific address, so step one is confirming you're actually inside a delivery zone. Use the official locator, or start from our store locator to zero in on your city and get pointed the right way. And here's an honest heads-up nobody likes to hear — not every address makes the cut. If you live way out in the countryside or on the far edge of a coverage map, you might be carryout-only. It's not personal, it's just how the delivery zones fall, and it's far better to know that before you've got your heart set on a doorstep pizza that isn't coming.

How Long You'll Actually Wait

Most delivery orders land somewhere in that 25-to-40-minute window, which is honestly pretty solid for hot food to your door. But let's be real about when it stretches, because managing your expectations saves a lot of frustration.

When You OrderTypical WaitWhy
Weekday, off-peak20–30 minStores are quiet, drivers are free
Friday / Saturday dinner rush35–50 minEveryone orders at once
Big game or holiday45–60+ minPeak demand, limited drivers
Bad weatherAdd 10–20 minSlower, more careful driving

The app's live tracker walks you through every stage, from the dough being prepped to your driver pulling out of the lot, so you're never left standing by the window guessing. If timing is tight — say you've got hungry kids or people arriving — ordering a little earlier than you think you need to is always the smart move.

The Fee Nobody Loves (and How It Breaks Down)

Expect a delivery fee somewhere in the four-to-six-dollar range, set by your local store. And this next part is important, so I'm going to say it as plainly as I possibly can: that fee is not a tip. Your driver does not pocket it. It goes to the store to cover the cost of running delivery. So if you can swing it, tip your driver separately (our tipping guide has the actual amounts) — they're the actual reason your dinner arrived warm instead of lukewarm, and they're very often driving their own car and paying for their own gas to do it.

ChargeRoughlyWho Gets It
Delivery fee$3.99–$5.99The store, not the driver
Tip (recommended)15–20% or a few dollarsYour driver
Small-order surchargeVariesThe store, if below the minimum

How Much Should You Tip?

A fair rule is 15 to 20 percent of the order, or a few dollars minimum on a smaller one, and bump it up in rotten weather or for a long drive. Drivers work hard for reasonable pay, and a decent tip genuinely matters to them. It's the part of the bill I'd cut last, not first.

Tracking It Down to the Minute

Give Domino's credit here — the Tracker is genuinely one of the better ordering tools any chain has ever built. It shows your pizza moving through prep, into the oven, past the quality check, and finally out the door with a named driver, all updating in real time. It's oddly satisfying to watch, honestly, and it takes the anxiety out of the wait. The stages are simple: your order is prepped, then baked, then given a quick quality check, then handed to a driver for delivery. When you see that last stage flip, it's time to make sure someone's near the door. A quick tip — double-check your address and any gate codes before you submit, since a wrong detail is the number-one reason a smooth order suddenly goes sideways.

Delivery vs Carryout: The Honest Comparison

Real talk, because I'd rather be honest than flattering — delivery will always cost more than carryout once that fee and a fair tip stack up. There's simply no way around it. Here's the trade-off laid bare.

FactorDeliveryCarryout
Extra feesDelivery fee + tipNone
Exclusive dealsFewerCarryout-only specials
ConvenienceHighest — you don't moveA short trip
Best forBad weather, no car, pure comfortSaving money

If you can possibly pick it up yourself, a carryout deal beats delivery every single time, no contest.

How to Spend Less on Delivery

Sometimes you're just set on delivery, and that's completely fair — that's kind of the whole appeal. When you go that route, do this to soften the cost: order through Mix & Match to lock in low per-item pricing, hit any delivery minimum efficiently rather than padding your cart with junk you won't eat, and stay signed into Domino's Rewards so the order still earns toward a free pizza later. Choosing a large over a medium also stretches your money further per slice. You'll never make delivery cheaper than carryout, but you can absolutely make it hurt a lot less. The complete system is in the money-saving guide.

Late-Night Cravings, Covered

Here's one of Domino's genuinely underrated strengths. A lot of stores deliver late — frequently till midnight, sometimes all the way to one in the morning — which makes it the reliable go-to when basically nothing else is open and you're wide awake and hungry. We've all been there at least once. Just confirm your specific store's hours on the hours page or directly in the app, because closing times swing quite a bit by location, and you don't want to place a mental order for a store that shut twenty minutes ago.

Common Delivery Problems (and Quick Fixes)

Even a great system hiccups now and then. If your pizza shows up cold, it's usually a long drive or a delay on your end getting to the door — the tracker helps you catch it coming. If something's wrong or missing from the order, the app and the store can sort it out, so hang onto your order confirmation. And if the driver can't find you, a clear address, a unit number, and a quick note about the buzzer or gate solves it before it starts. Little bits of prep on your side keep the whole thing smooth. If something does go wrong, our guide to wrong, late and missing orders walks through exactly who to contact and what you are entitled to.

Order With Confidence

Delivery availability, timing, and fees are all set by individual franchises and shift constantly with demand, so let the checkout screen confirm the real details before you commit. This is an independent, unofficial guide, written purely to help you order smarter and spend less — not to take your order or quote you a guaranteed price. And when you're ready to plan the actual food, swing by our Domino's menu with prices guide for the full rundown of what everything costs. Now go get that pizza. You've earned it.
