content:
Domino's Finally Made a Stuffed Crust

For years there was one obvious question in the Domino's app that had a disappointing answer: where's the stuffed crust? Pizza Hut had owned that idea since the nineties, and Domino's simply didn't have one. That changed in March 2025, when Domino's launched Parmesan Stuffed Crust — the first stuffed crust in the company's history, and a permanent menu item rather than a limited-time test.

So it's real, it's not going anywhere, and the question now is a practical one: what does it cost, which size can you get it in, how many calories does it add, and is it actually worth the upcharge over the crust you already order? Let's go through all of it properly. And the usual honest note first — every price here is an example, because Domino's stores are individually franchised and price independently. The checkout screen is the only number that counts.

What's Actually Inside the Crust

The name is slightly misleading, so let's clear it up straight away. The cheese stuffed inside the rim is mozzarella — 100% real mozzarella, baked into a buttery-flavoured dough. The Parmesan is on the outside: the crust is finished with Domino's garlic seasoning and a sprinkle of Parmesan across the top of the rim.

That's a meaningful difference from what most people picture. This isn't a Parmesan-filled crust; it's a mozzarella-filled crust wearing a garlic-Parmesan coat. And that outer seasoning is genuinely what makes it taste different from every other crust on the menu — you get savoury, garlicky, slightly salty edges rather than the plain bread rim you'd normally leave on the plate.

Domino's Stuffed Crust Price

Here's roughly what to expect. Remember these move by location.

OrderSizeExample Price
Cheese, Parmesan Stuffed CrustMedium 12"~$10.99
One topping, Parmesan Stuffed CrustMedium 12"~$10.99–$12.99
Mix & Match, 2-topping, 2+ pizzasMedium 12"~$10.99 each
Same pizza on Hand TossedMedium 12"~$9.99–$10.99

The number that actually matters is the gap, and the stuffed crust upcharge typically lands between about $1 and $3 per pizza. On one pizza that's nothing — it's less than a dipping cup. On a family order of four pizzas it's a real $8 to $12, which is worth thinking about before you tap it on every pie out of habit. Our money-saving playbook covers where else that money leaks.

Which Sizes Can You Get It In?

This is the most common point of confusion, so let me be precise about what's known and what varies.

Parmesan Stuffed Crust launched on the medium 12-inch, and medium remains the core size at most stores. Promotions have periodically opened it up more widely — Domino's added it to a $9.99 "any crust, any toppings" offer, for example — but that isn't the same as it being permanently available in every size everywhere.

The reliable test takes ten seconds: open the app, choose your size first, then look at the crust list. If Parmesan Stuffed Crust greys out when you switch to large, your store doesn't offer it in that size. That beats any chart on the internet, including this one. If you're weighing sizes generally, our pizza sizes and prices guide breaks down what each one actually feeds.

Calories: The Honest Number

Cheese baked into the rim isn't free, and this is where stuffed crust asks the most of you.

Parmesan Stuffed Crust, pepperoni~330 cal~2,640 cal

So you're paying roughly 100 extra calories per slice versus Hand Tossed — around 800 across a medium pizza. A medium stuffed crust pizza carries more total calories than a large Hand Tossed cheese pizza does. That's not a reason to avoid it; it's a reason to treat it as the indulgent order it is, rather than your default. Full numbers for every crust and size are in our Domino's calories and nutrition guide.

How It Stacks Up Against the Other Crusts

Domino's now has six crusts, and stuffed crust sits at one clear end of the range.

CrustTextureSizesBest For
Crunchy ThinCrisp, cracker-likeS / M / LLightest option
Hand TossedSoft, chewyS / M / LThe everyday default

Parmesan StuffedFilled, seasoned rimM (check store)Making the crust the point

The honest framing is that Parmesan Stuffed Crust and Handmade Pan compete for the same job — the treat pizza. Pan gives you a thick, buttery base; stuffed crust gives you a filled, seasoned edge. If you're the person who eats the crust first, stuffed wins. If you want richness throughout the whole slice, Pan is your pizza. Our crust types guide covers all six in detail.

Domino's vs Pizza Hut Stuffed Crust

You can't write about this without addressing the comparison everyone makes, so here it is fairly.

Pizza Hut has had stuffed crust for decades and it's the benchmark — a simple cheese-filled rim that delivers a clean cheese pull. Domino's took a different angle, layering garlic seasoning and Parmesan across the top of the rim, so the edge tastes seasoned and savoury rather than purely cheesy.

Neither is objectively better; they're aiming at different cravings. If what you want is the pure nostalgic cheese pull, Pizza Hut still owns that. If you like garlic-butter breadstick flavour and want your crust to actually taste of something, the Domino's version is the more interesting one. Where Domino's usually has the advantage is on the surrounding order — the deals and coupons and the rewards programme tend to make the total cheaper.

Which Toppings Work Best on It

Stuffed crust changes the balance of the pizza, so a couple of pairings work noticeably better than others:

  • Pepperoni — the classic, and the salt plays well with the garlic-Parmesan edge
  • Plain cheese — lets the crust be the whole point, which is arguably why you ordered it
  • Italian sausage and peppers — savoury enough to keep up with a seasoned rim
  • Anything sweet, like pineapple — genuinely divisive here; the garlic seasoning fights the sweetness
  • Heavily loaded meat combinations — the pizza gets very rich very fast when the crust is already filled

One practical tip: because the rim is doing so much work, ordering fewer toppings than usual is not a downgrade on this crust. A one-topping stuffed crust often eats better than a four-topping one, and it keeps you inside the cheaper deal tiers.

How to Order It (and the Deals to Watch)

It's a crust option, not a separate menu item, which trips people up when they go hunting for it under specialty pizzas.

  • Start a build-your-own pizza in the app or on the website, not a specialty recipe
  • Pick your size first — medium is the safest bet for availability
  • Choose Parmesan Stuffed Crust from the crust list, then add toppings
  • Check the deals tab before you pay — the same pizza is often cheaper inside an active offer

On deals specifically: Domino's has run Parmesan Stuffed Crust inside its $9.99 Best Deal Ever promotion at no extra charge, and it regularly appears in Mix & Match style pricing at around $10.99 each on two-topping pizzas. Those offers rotate and expire, so treat the current coupons page as the source of truth, and read our Mix & Match explainer if you want to understand how the multi-pizza pricing actually works. Carryout is worth a look too — the carryout deals guide covers where pickup beats delivery pricing.

So Is It Worth It?

Here's the straight verdict, split by who's asking.

Order it if you're buying one or two pizzas as a treat, you actually eat the crust rather than leaving a graveyard of rims in the box, or you've been ordering elsewhere purely because Domino's didn't have a stuffed crust. A dollar or two for a filled, seasoned edge is decent value, and it turns the least interesting part of the pizza into the best part.

Skip it if you're feeding a crowd and the upcharge multiplies across four or five pizzas, you're watching calories closely, or you're the sort who leaves the crust anyway — in which case you'd be paying extra for the bit you don't eat. In those cases Hand Tossed remains the smarter buy, and Crunchy Thin the lighter one.

What's not in doubt is that it fills a real gap. Domino's went years without an answer to the most-requested crust in the category, and now there's one worth ordering on purpose. Browse the rest of the lineup with example prices on our Domino's menu with prices page — and as always, confirm the final number at checkout.

title: Domino's Order Wrong, Late or Missing? (2026): What to Actually Do
excerpt: The practical steps when a Domino's order arrives wrong, cold, late or not at all — which programme covers what, the compensation choice most people get wrong, and how to complain in a way that actually gets resolved.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: A Domino's delivery order at the door, illustrating what to do when something goes wrong
keywords: does Domino's still do 30 minutes or free

faqs.question: What do I do if my Domino's order is wrong?
faqs.answer: Contact the store you ordered from before you eat it, with your order number ready. Most stores will remake the item or refund it. Take a photo first — it takes five seconds and it removes any argument about what actually arrived.

faqs.question: Does Domino's give refunds?
faqs.answer: Yes. Domino's policy covers refunds where an order arrives damaged, incorrect or otherwise not as it should be. Whether you get a refund, a remake or store credit depends on the situation and the store, and asking politely for the one you'd prefer usually works.

faqs.question: What is Domino's Carryout Insurance?
faqs.answer: A free programme covering carryout orders damaged after you leave the store — the classic case being a box that slides off the seat. Bring it back within two hours to the store you bought it from and they remake it. It's replaced like for like, so no swapping it for something different.

faqs.question: What is Domino's Delivery Insurance?
faqs.answer: A programme for delivery orders that arrive not as they should. You report the problem through the Domino's tracker, your order confirmation page or the confirmation email, and you're offered a choice of compensation — typically a 20% off coupon for your next order or 60 rewards points.

faqs.question: Should I take the coupon or the points?
faqs.answer: Usually the points, and it isn't close. 60 points is the threshold for a free medium two-topping pizza, worth roughly $11 to $13. A 20% coupon on a $25 order saves you $5. Most people take the coupon because it sounds more immediate, and leave about half the value behind.

faqs.question: Does Domino's still do 30 minutes or free?
faqs.answer: No, not in the United States. Domino's dropped the 30-minute delivery guarantee back in 1993 following lawsuits related to drivers rushing. There is no automatic compensation for a late delivery today — if a delay is unreasonable you can raise it, but the guarantee no longer exists.

faqs.question: My order never arrived at all. What now?
faqs.answer: Call the store directly rather than using the app — it's faster and someone there can see the order and the driver. Have your order number ready. If the order genuinely never arrived, a refund or a remake is the normal outcome.

faqs.question: I ordered through DoorDash and it was wrong. Who do I contact?
faqs.answer: The app, not Domino's. When you order through a third-party platform, your contract is with that platform, it processed your payment, and Domino's has no ability to refund it. Going to the store first just adds a step.

faqs.question: Will complaining get the driver in trouble?
faqs.answer: Not if you're accurate about what went wrong. A missing item was packed at the store, a long wait is usually the kitchen. Say what actually happened rather than which person you dealt with, and the complaint lands where the problem was.

faqs.question: How long do I have to report a problem?
faqs.answer: Sooner is better in every case, and Carryout Insurance specifically runs on a two-hour window. For delivery issues, report it the same evening while the order is still live in the system — a complaint a week later is much harder for anyone to verify or resolve.

content:
First: Where Did You Order From?

Before anything else, answer this, because it decides the entire process and people waste a lot of time getting it wrong.

You ordered viaWho fixes it
Domino's app or websiteThe Domino's store
Domino's phone orderThe Domino's store
DoorDash, Grubhub, Uber EatsThe delivery app

If you ordered through a third-party platform, Domino's cannot refund you. That platform took your payment, holds the contract, and runs its own refunds process. Calling the store first just adds a step before you end up in the app anyway.

The rest of this page assumes you ordered direct.

Do This Before You Do Anything Else

  • Take a photo. Five seconds, and it ends any disagreement about what arrived. This matters most for wrong items and damaged boxes
  • Don't eat it yet. Awkward, but a remake is much easier to arrange when the item still exists
  • Find your order number. It's on the confirmation email and in the app. Every conversation goes faster with it
  • Note the time. Relevant for carryout, which runs on a clock

Delivery Problems: The Insurance Programme

Domino's runs a Delivery Insurance programme for orders that arrive not as they should. The useful thing is where you report it: through the Domino's tracker, your order confirmation page, or the confirmation email — not by hunting for a general contact form.

You're then offered a choice of compensation, typically a 20% off coupon for your next order or 60 rewards points.

Take the points

This is the single most useful thing on this page, and most people get it backwards.

OptionWhat it's worth
20% off your next order~$5 on a $25 order
60 rewards pointsA free medium 2-topping pizza, ~$11–$13

60 points is the redemption threshold for a free pizza in Domino's Rewards. The points are worth roughly double the coupon, and they don't oblige you to spend anything to use them — a percentage-off coupon only pays out if you order again, and only in proportion to how much you spend.

The coupon feels more immediate, which is why people take it. Our rewards guide covers the redemption tiers if you want to check the maths against your own ordering pattern.

Carryout Problems: The Two-Hour Window

Domino's Carryout Insurance covers orders damaged after you leave the store — the box sliding off the passenger seat being the classic case. It's free and it applies to all carryout orders.

The rules that matter:

  • Two hours from purchase
  • The same store you bought it from
  • Bring the order back — they need to see it
  • Like-for-like replacement. Same products, no substitutions, so you can't upgrade to something else

Worth knowing this exists, because a lot of people write off a dropped pizza as their own fault and eat the loss. It's a genuinely generous programme and it's underused.

Wrong or Missing Items

The most common problem, and usually the easiest to fix.

Call the store directly. Not the app, not corporate — the store that made your food. They have the order in front of them, they can see what was packed, and they can act immediately. The app is slower for this because it routes rather than resolves.

Typical outcomes:

  • Missing item: sent out, or refunded
  • Wrong item: remade, or refunded
  • Wrong toppings: remade — this is where your photo helps

A note on tone that genuinely changes the result: lead with what happened rather than what you want. "The order was meant to have two pizzas and only one arrived" gets a faster resolution than opening with a demand, because the person answering can act on the first and has to negotiate the second.

Late Orders, and the 30-Minute Question

People still ask about this, so let's settle it: Domino's no longer offers "30 minutes or free" in the United States. The guarantee was dropped in 1993 after lawsuits connected to drivers rushing to meet it. It's been gone for decades.

Which means there's no automatic compensation for a late delivery. A long wait on a Friday night is usually the kitchen being busy, and that isn't a fault so much as a queue.

What is worth raising:

  • An estimate that was wildly wrong — quoted 30 minutes, arrived in 90
  • Food that arrived cold as a result of the delay
  • A tracker that showed the order as delivered when it hadn't been

Those are service failures rather than a slow night, and stores generally respond to them.

How to Escalate

In order. Skipping steps usually makes it slower, not faster.

  • 1. The store. Resolves the overwhelming majority of problems, immediately
  • 2. The tracker or confirmation email for the insurance programmes
  • 3. Domino's customer service if the store won't help — franchises are independently run and standards vary, and corporate does want to know when one falls short

When you escalate, include: order number, store number and address, date and time, what went wrong, what you'd like done, and photos. A message with those six things gets handled. A message that says the food was bad does not.

What You're Owed vs What's Goodwill

Worth being clear-eyed about, because it shapes how you ask.

SituationReasonable expectation
Wrong item deliveredRemake or refund
Item missing entirelyRemake or refund
Order never arrivedRefund
Carryout damaged, within 2 hoursFree remake
Delivery arrived poorlyInsurance compensation
Slow on a busy nightGoodwill, if anything
You didn't enjoy itGoodwill, if anything

The top half is a fault that should be put right. The bottom half is a request. Both are fine to raise — but knowing which one you're making tends to produce a better conversation.

Keep the Driver Out of It

One thing worth separating, because it costs people money unfairly.

A missing item was packed at the store. A long wait was the kitchen. A cold pizza on a long route is distance. None of those are the driver, and reducing a tip to punish a store error takes it out of the wrong person's pay — a meaningful share of a driver's earnings comes from tips, as our tipping guide covers.

Report the fault to the store, tip the driver for the part they did. If the driver genuinely was the problem — rude, or clearly took a detour — that's different, and worth saying plainly.

The Short Version

Photo first, order number ready, call the store. Third-party app orders go through the app, not Domino's. Carryout damage has a two-hour window. And if you're offered a coupon or points, take the points — they're worth about double.

Programmes and policies vary between franchised stores and change over time, so treat this as a guide to how the process generally works rather than a guarantee. This is an independent, unofficial site with no connection to Domino's — we can't resolve an order, and our contact page explains what we can and can't help with.

title: How Much to Tip Domino's Delivery (2026): A Straight Answer
excerpt: What to actually tip a Domino's driver, why the delivery fee doesn't count toward it, when to tip more than usual, whether carryout needs a tip, and what tips are really worth to the person at your door.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Domino's delivery order at a doorstep, illustrating a guide to tipping drivers
keywords: how much to tip Domino's delivery
does the delivery fee go to the driver

faqs.question: How much should I tip a Domino's delivery driver?
faqs.answer: The common US convention is 15 to 20 percent of the food subtotal before fees and tax, with a floor of about $3 to $5 whatever the order size. On a $20 order that's roughly $3 to $4; over $20, most people treat $5 as the sensible minimum.

faqs.question: Doesn't the delivery fee already cover the tip?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the single most common misunderstanding about pizza delivery. Domino's says plainly in its own FAQ that the delivery charge is not a tip to the driver. It goes to the store to cover the costs of running a delivery operation — insurance, hot bags, extra staff, vehicle costs — not to the person who brought your food.

faqs.question: Do I need to tip for carryout?
faqs.answer: No. Carryout involves no driver, no vehicle and no trip to your address, and nobody expects a tip for handing you a box at the counter. Some people leave something small if staff have gone out of their way, but it is genuinely optional in a way that delivery tipping is not.

faqs.question: Is it better to tip in cash or in the app?
faqs.answer: Either works, and the in-app tip reaches the driver. Cash has the advantage of being immediate and unambiguous, and plenty of drivers prefer it for that reason. What matters far more than the method is that a tip exists at all.

faqs.question: How much of a driver's income comes from tips?
faqs.answer: A large share. For many delivery drivers tips account for roughly 30 to 60 percent of what they take home on a shift, on top of an hourly wage. That is why skipping the tip because the delivery fee looked expensive has a much bigger effect on the driver than most customers realise.

faqs.question: Should I tip more in bad weather?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's the situation where it matters most. Snow, ice, storms and extreme heat make the job slower and genuinely unpleasant, usually in the driver's own car. Adding $3 to $5, or moving to 25 percent, is the normal response.

faqs.question: What if my order arrives late or cold?
faqs.answer: Consider whether it was actually the driver's doing. A long wait is usually the kitchen being busy, and a cold pizza on a long route is often distance rather than dawdling. If the driver was polite and did their part, tip normally and take the service problem to the store — the driver is rarely the person who caused it.

faqs.question: Do drivers get paid for mileage?
faqs.answer: It varies, and that's the honest answer. Domino's stores are individually franchised, so some reimburse mileage, some provide vehicles and some do neither. Many drivers use their own cars and cover fuel and wear themselves, which is worth remembering on a long delivery.

faqs.question: Is tipping actually required?
faqs.answer: It isn't a rule, and nobody will stop you at the door. It is a strong social convention in the United States, and driver pay is structured around the assumption that it happens. Treat it as part of the cost of having food brought to you rather than as an optional extra.

faqs.question: What's the cheapest honest way to avoid tipping?
faqs.answer: Carryout. It removes the driver from the transaction entirely, so there's nobody to tip, and it removes the delivery fee at the same time. If the tip is the part of the bill you want to avoid, collecting the order yourself is the straightforward answer rather than under-tipping someone.

content:
The Short Answer

Tip 15 to 20 percent of the food subtotal, with a floor of about $3 to $5 no matter how small the order is. On a normal weeknight pizza that usually means $3 to $5. Add a few dollars on top in bad weather, for a long drive, or if getting to your door is awkward.

Order subtotalReasonable tip
Up to $20$3–$4
$20–$40$5–$8
$40–$8015–20%
$80–$150 (group order)$15–$20 minimum
Bad weather, long distanceAdd $3–$5
CarryoutNothing expected

That's the practical answer. The rest of this page is why, because the reasoning changes how people tip more than the number does.

The Delivery Fee Is Not a Tip

This is the misunderstanding that costs drivers the most money, and it is completely understandable — you pay a charge with the word "delivery" on it, so you reasonably assume it pays for the delivery.

It doesn't. Domino's says so itself. Its own FAQ states plainly that the delivery charge is not a tip to the driver. The fee, typically somewhere in the four-to-six-dollar range and set independently by each franchised store, goes to the store to cover the cost of running a delivery operation — insurance, hot bags, extra staff on the roster, vehicle costs.

So the fee and the tip are two separate things paying for two separate parts of the transaction. Our delivery guide breaks down the fee itself in more detail if you want the full picture of what you're being charged.

Worth knowing: Domino's has at times run promotions rewarding customers for tipping their driver. A company designing a campaign around encouraging tips is a fairly clear signal about where the fee is not going.

What a Tip Is Actually Worth to the Driver

Some context that makes the numbers make sense.

Domino's drivers are employees rather than gig workers, so there is an hourly wage underneath. But for many delivery drivers, tips make up somewhere around 30 to 60 percent of what they take home on a shift. That is not a rounding error — it is a substantial part of the job's actual pay.

Add to that a detail people rarely think about: a lot of drivers use their own cars. Whether mileage is reimbursed varies by store, because every Domino's is independently franchised — some reimburse, some provide vehicles, some do neither. When it isn't reimbursed, fuel and wear on a personal car come out of the same money the tips are part of.

None of this is an argument that you owe anyone a specific amount. It's context for why $3 on a $20 order is normal and $0 lands differently than it feels from the customer's side of the door.

Working Out the Number

Two rules, and the higher one wins:

  • Percentage: 15 to 20 percent of the food subtotal — before fees and before tax, not after
  • Floor: at least $3 to $5, regardless of how small the order is

The floor matters more than people expect. A driver making a fifteen-minute round trip for a single small pizza has done almost the same work as one delivering forty dollars of food, so percentage alone under-pays small orders badly. Ten percent of a $12 pizza is $1.20, which is not really a tip.

Calculating on the subtotal rather than the total is also deliberate. Tipping on top of tax and the delivery fee means tipping on money the driver never sees.

When to Add More

Situations where the standard number is too low:

  • Bad weather. Snow, ice, storms, extreme heat. This is the big one — the job gets slower, harder and less safe, in the driver's own car. Add $3 to $5, or go to 25 percent
  • Long distance. If you are at the edge of the delivery zone, that's a real drive each way
  • Hard-to-reach doors. A fifth-floor walk-up, a building with no lift access for drivers, a long car park, a gated complex where they had to wait
  • Large group orders. Five to nine pizzas is heavy, awkward and often several trips from the car. $15 to $20 is the floor there
  • Peak nights. Friday and Saturday evenings, big game days, holidays
  • They did something helpful. Carried it upstairs, waited while you found your keys, remembered your building

Cash or In-App?

Both work, and the in-app tip does reach the driver. The practical differences:

In-app is convenient, you don't need change, and it's recorded. Cash is immediate and unambiguous, and plenty of drivers prefer it for exactly that reason.

One small thing in favour of cash: if you're unsure what the wait will be like and want to decide when the food actually arrives, cash lets you tip based on what happened rather than what you guessed at checkout. But this is a preference, not a rule — the method matters far less than whether there is a tip at all.

Carryout: You Don't Need to Tip

Straightforward answer: no tip is expected on carryout. There is no driver, no vehicle and no trip to your address. Somebody hands you a box over a counter.

Some people leave something small if staff have been notably helpful, or drop change into a tip jar if one exists, and that's a kindness rather than an obligation. This is genuinely different from delivery, where the pay structure assumes tipping happens.

Which points at something useful: if the tip is the part of the bill you'd rather not pay, carryout is the honest way to avoid it. You skip the tip and the delivery fee together, and nobody is short-changed for it. Our carryout guide works through what that's worth on a normal order — it's usually more than people assume.

When Something Goes Wrong

The order arrives late, or cold, or an item is missing. Should the tip absorb that?

Usually not, and it's worth separating who did what:

  • A long wait is nearly always the kitchen being busy, not the driver being slow
  • A missing item was packed at the store, not chosen by the driver
  • A cold pizza on a long route is distance and physics more often than dawdling
  • A driver who was rude, or clearly took a detour, is a genuine reason to tip low — that one is on them

The general principle: tip the driver for the part of the job the driver controls, and take the service problem to the store. Domino's has a complaints process and it works better than withholding five dollars from someone who didn't cause the problem.

Quick Reference

SituationWhat to do
Normal weeknight, one pizza$3–$5
Family order, $50 or so15–20%, about $8–$10
Office order, $120$15–$20 minimum
SnowstormUsual amount plus $3–$5
Fifth-floor walk-upUsual amount plus a few dollars
CarryoutNothing
Order late, driver was fineTip normally, complain to the store
Driver was rudeTip low, and tell the store why

The Honest Summary

Tipping isn't a rule and nobody is going to enforce it. But driver pay in the US is built on the assumption that it happens, the delivery fee genuinely doesn't reach the driver, and a meaningful share of what they earn on a shift arrives at your door rather than in their paycheque.

Three to five dollars on a normal order, fifteen to twenty percent on a bigger one, more when the weather or the building makes it hard. And if you'd rather not tip at all, that's a completely reasonable position — collect the order yourself, and you've dodged the fee as well.

This is an independent guide, not Domino's. Fees, wages and reimbursement policies vary between franchised stores, and tipping conventions are norms rather than requirements. For what the delivery fee itself covers, see our Domino's delivery guide; for spending less on the whole order, the money-saving playbook.

title: Domino's Crust Types Explained (2026): Which One Should You Order?
excerpt: Hand Tossed, Pan, Thin, Brooklyn or Gluten Free? A no-nonsense breakdown of every Domino's crust — taste, texture, sizes and which one actually suits your order.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Domino's pizzas showing different crust types side by side

faqs.question: What is the best Domino's crust?
faqs.answer: It depends on your taste. Hand Tossed is the safe crowd-pleaser, Handmade Pan is the indulgent one, and Crunchy Thin is best if you find most pizza too bready. There's no single winner — just the right one for your mood.

faqs.question: What is the default Domino's crust?
faqs.answer: Hand Tossed is the default. It's soft, a little chewy, and works with just about any topping combination, which is why most people stick with it.

faqs.question: Which Domino's crust is thickest?
faqs.answer: Handmade Pan is the thickest and richest, baked in a pan for a buttery, crisp bottom. It's only available in Small and Medium.

faqs.question: Is Brooklyn Style crust thin or thick?
faqs.answer: Brooklyn Style is thin, big and foldable — cut into large New-York-style slices. It scales up to Extra Large, so it's the choice for maximum pizza.

faqs.question: Which crust has the fewest calories?
faqs.answer: Crunchy Thin generally has the fewest calories because it uses the least dough. Pairing it with light cheese trims things down further.

faqs.question: Does Domino's have a gluten-free crust?
faqs.answer: Yes, a Small Gluten Free crust. Domino's prepares it in a shared kitchen, so it suits a preference rather than a severe gluten allergy or celiac disease.

faqs.question: Do all crusts come in every size?
faqs.answer: No. Hand Tossed and Crunchy Thin come in Small, Medium and Large; Handmade Pan is Small and Medium only; Brooklyn Style is Large and Extra Large; Gluten Free is Small only.

content:
The Crust Decision People Rush

Here's a little thing that changes your whole pizza and almost nobody thinks about it: the crust. Most people tap Hand Tossed on autopilot and move on. And look, Hand Tossed is great — but if you've never tried the others, you're missing out on how different the same pizza can taste. Let's fix that. I'll walk you through all six Domino's crusts, honestly, so next time you order on purpose instead of out of habit.

Hand Tossed — The Reliable Default

This is the one you already know. Soft, a touch chewy, with a lightly seasoned edge. It comes in Small, Medium and Large, and it plays nice with every topping combination on the menu. If you're feeding a group with mixed tastes, Hand Tossed is the peacekeeper — nobody ever complains about it. It's my default when I'm not in the mood to think about it, and honestly that's most nights.

Handmade Pan — The Indulgent One

Now we're talking treat territory. Handmade Pan is baked right in the pan, which gives it a thick, pillowy middle and a buttery, crisp golden bottom. It's richer and heavier than the rest, so it's the crust I reach for when I want pizza to feel like an event rather than just dinner. The catch? It only comes in Small and Medium — no Large — so it's better for one or two people than a big crowd.

Crunchy Thin — For the Anti-Bread Crowd

If you've ever thought 'there's too much bread on this pizza,' Crunchy Thin is your answer. It's light, crisp, almost cracker-like, and it lets the sauce and toppings do all the talking. It also tends to be the lowest-calorie option because there's simply less dough — our Domino's calories and nutrition guide has the per-slice numbers for every crust. Great for a loaded specialty pizza where a thick crust would be overkill. Just know it's fragile — it won't fold, it'll snap.

Brooklyn Style — Big and Foldable

This one's for the New-York-slice fans. Brooklyn Style is thin but sturdy, stretched wide and cut into large slices you can actually fold in half street-vendor style. It's the only crust that scales up to Extra Large (16 inches), so it's the move when you want the most pizza in a single pie. There's something genuinely fun about folding a Brooklyn slice — it eats differently from everything else here.

Gluten Free — The Careful Choice

Domino's offers a Small Gluten Free crust for anyone avoiding wheat. It's a real option and it tastes good, but I have to be straight with you: it's made in a shared kitchen, so it isn't suitable for a severe gluten allergy or celiac disease. Treat it as a preference-friendly choice rather than a medically safe one, and when in doubt, ask the store about their process.

Parmesan Stuffed Crust — The New One

Domino's went decades without a stuffed crust, and then in 2025 it finally arrived. Parmesan Stuffed Crust is a buttery-flavoured dough with real mozzarella baked inside the rim, finished on top with garlic seasoning and a sprinkle of Parmesan. It turns the part of the pizza most people leave on the plate into the bit they fight over. It usually costs a dollar or two more than the others and runs about 100 calories more per slice, and medium is the size to look for. If you're curious, we've covered it properly in our Parmesan Stuffed Crust guide.

Quick Comparison

Still deciding? Here's the whole lineup at a glance.

CrustTextureSizesBest For
Hand TossedSoft, chewyS / M / LEveryone, every night
Handmade PanThick, butteryS / MA proper treat
Crunchy ThinLight, crispS / M / LLess bread, more toppings
Brooklyn StyleThin, foldableL / XLNY-style, big appetites
Gluten FreeFirm, crispSmall onlyAvoiding wheat
Parmesan StuffedFilled, seasoned rimMediumMaking the crust the point

So Which One Should You Order?

Let me make it simple. Feeding a mixed group? Hand Tossed. Want to treat yourself? Handmade Pan. Ordering a loaded specialty and want the toppings to shine? Crunchy Thin. Chasing that foldable pizzeria vibe or feeding a crowd? Brooklyn Style. Avoiding wheat? Gluten Free, with the shared-kitchen caveat in mind. None of these cost more than the base pizza price (except a small gluten-free upcharge), so trying a new one is basically free experimentation.

Pair It Right

Crust choice pairs with size, so it's worth reading the pizza sizes guide alongside this one — a Large Brooklyn eats very differently from a Medium Pan. And whatever you pick, order it through a value deal so you're not paying full price. For the whole lineup and what it costs, the menu with prices page has you covered.

The Bottom Line

The crust is the easiest way to make the same Domino's pizza feel brand new. Five options, no extra cost to speak of, wildly different results. Pick on purpose next time and you'll notice the difference immediately. As always, this is an independent, unofficial guide — availability and any upcharge can vary by store, so verify at official checkout.

title: Domino's Vegetarian & Vegan Options (2026): What You Can Actually Order
excerpt: Domino's has no vegan cheese in the US — but you can still eat there. The honest guide to which crusts, sauces, toppings and sides are vegan, the much longer vegetarian list, and the cross-contact caveat nobody spells out.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: Overhead view of a Domino's order with a vegetable-topped pizza and sides

pricing.item: Build-your-own pasta, tomato sauce, no cheese

faqs.question: Does Domino's have vegan cheese?
faqs.answer: Not in the US. As of 2026 Domino's USA does not carry a vegan cheese alternative or a meatless pepperoni, so a vegan pizza has to be ordered with no cheese at all. Some Domino's markets outside the US do offer vegan cheese, which is why you'll see conflicting answers online.

faqs.question: Which Domino's crusts are vegan?
faqs.answer: Hand Tossed, Crunchy Thin and Brooklyn Style are generally made without dairy or egg. Handmade Pan is not — it contains milk. Parmesan Stuffed Crust obviously isn't either, since cheese is baked into the rim. Ingredients can change, so check the current list if it matters to you.

faqs.question: Which Domino's sauce is vegan?
faqs.answer: Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce is the reliable vegan choice, and it also works as a pasta base. The creamy sauces — Alfredo, ranch and garlic Parmesan — all contain dairy, so they're out.

faqs.question: How do you order a vegan pizza at Domino's?
faqs.answer: Start a build-your-own pizza, choose Hand Tossed, Thin or Brooklyn Style, select Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce, set cheese to none, then add whichever vegetable toppings you want. That's the whole method — the no-cheese step is the one people forget.

faqs.question: Are Domino's bread twists vegan?
faqs.answer: No. The bread sides — Garlic and Parmesan Bread Twists, Parmesan Bread Bites, Stuffed Cheesy Bread and Cinnamon Bread Twists — all contain milk in their ingredient lists, so none of them are vegan. They are fine for most vegetarians.

faqs.question: What are the best vegetarian pizzas at Domino's?
faqs.answer: Pacific Veggie is the strongest — spinach, onions, mushrooms, tomatoes, black olives and feta with garlic herb seasoning. Spinach & Feta on an Alfredo base and Wisconsin 6 Cheese are the other two specialty pizzas with no meat on them.

faqs.question: Is Domino's pizza dough vegan?
faqs.answer: The Hand Tossed, Thin and Brooklyn Style doughs are generally free of dairy and egg, which makes them suitable for most vegans. The Handmade Pan dough contains milk. Domino's publishes an ingredient list, and that is the source worth checking before you order.

faqs.question: Can vegans eat Domino's pasta or salad?
faqs.answer: A build-your-own pasta with Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce and vegetable toppings, ordered without cheese, is the workable pasta option. For salad, the Classic Garden Salad works if you skip the cheddar and croutons and choose a vegan-friendly dressing such as balsamic vinaigrette.

faqs.question: Is Domino's safe for a strict vegan diet?
faqs.answer: Domino's does not market itself as vegan-friendly, and everything is prepared in a shared kitchen on shared surfaces with shared utensils. Cross-contact with cheese and meat is realistic. It suits a preference-based plant-based diet rather than a strict one, and only you can decide whether that threshold works for you.

faqs.question: Are Domino's desserts vegetarian or vegan?
faqs.answer: The Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes, Cinnamon Bread Twists and Marbled Cookie Brownie all contain dairy, so they are vegetarian but not vegan. There is currently no vegan dessert on the US menu.

content:
Let's Start With the Honest Part

If you're vegan and looking at the Domino's menu, here is the thing you need to know before anything else: Domino's in the US does not sell vegan cheese, and it does not sell a meatless pepperoni. As of 2026 there is no plant-based cheese alternative on the American menu at all.

So a vegan pizza from Domino's is a pizza with no cheese on it. That's the reality, and I'd rather tell you now than walk you through five sections before admitting it. Some Domino's markets outside the US do offer vegan cheese, which is why you'll find articles online that seem to say otherwise — those aren't describing the US menu.

The good news is that a no-cheese veggie pizza at Domino's is genuinely better than it sounds, and if you're vegetarian rather than vegan the menu opens up enormously. Let me walk through both, honestly, section by section. I cover ingredients and allergens for this site, and this is a topic where getting it slightly wrong actually matters — so I'll flag every place where you should verify rather than trust me.

Which Crusts Are Vegan?

Crust is the first decision and the one with a real trap in it.

CrustVegan?Note
Hand TossedGenerally yesThe default, no dairy or egg
Crunchy ThinGenerally yesThe lightest option
Brooklyn StyleGenerally yesLarge and XL only
Handmade PanNoContains milk
Parmesan Stuffed CrustNoCheese baked into the rim
Gluten FreeCheckVerify separately if you need both

Handmade Pan is the trap. It looks like plain dough and it isn't — it contains milk. If you order pan crust assuming it's just bread, you've made a mistake that's very easy to make. Our crust types guide covers how they differ in taste, and the gluten-free crust guide handles the wheat question separately.

Which Sauces Work?

Simple answer: Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce is your sauce. It's the standard pizza sauce, it's the vegan-friendly one, and it doubles as a pasta base.

What's out: Alfredo, ranch and garlic Parmesan are all dairy-based, so they're off the list for vegans entirely. They're fine for vegetarians. Honey BBQ is worth checking if honey is something you avoid.

You can also order light sauce, extra sauce or no sauce. If you're going cheeseless, extra sauce is the single best adjustment you can make — it stops the pizza drying out, which is the main complaint people have about no-cheese pizza. It's usually free, too. The full sauce lineup is in our toppings and prices guide.

Toppings You Can Use

This is where Domino's does reasonably well. The vegetable range is genuinely usable:

  • Mushrooms — meaty texture, the most useful topping on a cheeseless pizza
  • Onions — sweeten as they bake
  • Green peppers and roasted red peppers — the red ones are sweeter
  • Banana peppers and jalapeños — tang and heat respectively
  • Black olives and green olives — salt, which matters more without cheese
  • Baby spinach — wilts down nicely
  • Diced tomatoes — fresh contrast
  • Pineapple — your call
  • Garlic — cheap and does a lot of work

What's not available: any plant-based meat. There's no vegan pepperoni, sausage or chicken substitute on the US menu, so the protein options are limited to what the vegetables give you.

How to Build a Vegan Pizza, Step by Step

Four decisions, in this order:

  • 1. Crust — Hand Tossed, Crunchy Thin or Brooklyn Style
  • 2. Sauce — Robust Inspired Tomato, and consider extra
  • 3. Cheese — set it to none. This is the step people forget, and normal is the default
  • 4. Toppings — load up on vegetables; they're the cheapest toppings anyway

My honest recommendation for the best version: Hand Tossed, extra Robust Tomato, no cheese, mushrooms, onions, black olives, spinach and garlic. The olives and garlic supply the salt and savouriness the cheese would normally bring, and the extra sauce keeps it from being dry. It's a good pizza, not a consolation prize.

Vegan Sides — What's Actually Left

This part is thin, so let's be straight about it.

Build-your-own pasta works: choose Robust Inspired Tomato Sauce, add vegetable toppings, and order it with no cheese. It's the only real hot side available to a vegan.

Classic Garden Salad works if you skip the cheddar and the croutons, and choose a vegan-friendly dressing — balsamic vinaigrette is the usual pick. Check the dressing packet, because the creamy ones are out.

Everything in the bread category is out. Garlic Bread Twists, Parmesan Bread Twists, Parmesan Bread Bites, Stuffed Cheesy Bread and Cinnamon Bread Twists all contain milk. So do the desserts. There is currently no vegan dessert on the US menu. Prices for all of these are in our sides menu guide if you're ordering for a mixed group.

Vegetarian? The Menu Is Much Bigger

If dairy is fine and you're just avoiding meat, you have far more to work with.

CategoryVegetarian Options
Specialty pizzasPacific Veggie, Spinach & Feta, Wisconsin 6 Cheese
Build your ownCheese pizza plus any vegetable toppings
PastaPasta Primavera, or build your own without meat
SandwichesMediterranean Veggie
Bread sidesAll of them — twists, bites, Stuffed Cheesy Bread
SaladsClassic Garden Salad
DessertsLava cakes, Cinnamon Bread Twists, Cookie Brownie

Pacific Veggie is the standout — spinach, onions, mushrooms, tomatoes and black olives with feta and garlic herb seasoning. It's a proper pizza that happens to have no meat, not a cheese pizza with a couple of vegetables thrown at it. At roughly 230 calories a large slice it's also one of the lightest things on the menu. The full lineup is in our specialty pizzas guide.

One thing I genuinely can't answer for you: whether the cheese uses animal rennet. I couldn't verify that reliably, and I'm not going to guess on a question that decides whether some vegetarians can eat here at all. If it matters to you, ask Domino's directly rather than trusting any third-party page — including this one.

The Cross-Contact Reality

This needs saying plainly. Domino's does not market itself as vegan-friendly, and everything is made in a shared kitchen. The same surfaces, the same utensils, the same ovens, often the same hands between one pizza and the next.

So if you avoid animal products by preference, ethics or general diet, ordering cheeseless from Domino's is perfectly workable. If you need a guaranteed absence of dairy — a serious milk allergy, for instance — this isn't the right choice, and no amount of careful ordering changes that. It's the same caveat that applies to the gluten-free crust, and it comes from the same place: a fast, high-volume kitchen isn't built for separation.

Ordering Tips

A few things that make it go smoothly:

  • Check cheese is set to none before paying. Normal is the default and the builder won't warn you.
  • Add a note on the order. Not a guarantee, but it costs nothing and sometimes helps.
  • Order extra sauce. The single biggest improvement to a cheeseless pizza, and usually free.
  • Read the ingredient list yourself. Domino's publishes one, formulations change, and it beats any guide.
  • Deals still apply. A vegan build-your-own is a normal pizza as far as pricing goes — see the coupons page and the Mix & Match explainer.
  • Vegetables are the cheapest toppings. Loading up costs less than a meat pizza would.

The Verdict

For vegetarians, Domino's is straightforwardly fine — three meat-free specialty pizzas, a full vegetable range, pasta, a sandwich, every bread side and every dessert. You're not compromising much.

For vegans it's more limited, and I won't pretend otherwise: a cheeseless veggie pizza, a build-your-own pasta and a stripped-back salad is the whole list. No cheese alternative, no plant-based meat, no dessert. But the pizza itself is decent — load the vegetables, take the extra sauce, and it holds up better than most people expect.

Whether the shared kitchen is acceptable is a judgement only you can make. Everything else on the menu, with example prices, is on our Domino's menu with prices page — and as always, verify ingredients and the final total at checkout.

faqs.question: Is Domino's gluten-free crust safe for celiac disease?
faqs.answer: No. Domino's makes its gluten-free crust in a shared kitchen where wheat is present, so it isn't recommended for people with celiac disease or a severe gluten allergy. It's designed for those choosing to reduce gluten, not eliminate it entirely.

faqs.question: What size is Domino's gluten-free crust?
faqs.answer: It comes in a Small (10-inch) only. There is no medium or large gluten-free option.

faqs.question: Does the gluten-free crust cost extra?
faqs.answer: Usually a small upcharge over the standard crust, and prices vary by location. Verify the final total at official checkout.

faqs.question: Does gluten-free crust taste good?
faqs.answer: Most people find it genuinely enjoyable — crisp and firm, closer to a thin crust. It's a different texture from Hand Tossed, but a good one.

faqs.question: Can I put any toppings on gluten-free crust?
faqs.answer: You can add most standard toppings, but remember the toppings and sauces themselves may not all be gluten-free, and everything is prepared in a shared kitchen. Check individual ingredients if you're sensitive.

faqs.question: Is Domino's gluten-free crust vegan?
faqs.answer: The crust itself may not contain animal products, but cheese and many toppings do. Ask the store for current ingredient details if you're vegan or have other restrictions.

content:
Let's Be Honest About Gluten-Free Pizza

If you're avoiding gluten, you already know the drill — most 'gluten-free' menu items come with an asterisk. Domino's gluten-free crust is a genuinely welcome option, and it tastes good, but there's one important thing you need to understand before you order. So let's cover it plainly, no marketing spin, so you can make the right call for your own situation.

The Shared-Kitchen Caveat (Read This First)

Here's the part that matters most. Domino's prepares its gluten-free crust in the same kitchen where regular wheat dough is handled every day. That means cross-contact with gluten is possible. For that reason, Domino's itself does not recommend the gluten-free crust for people with celiac disease or a severe gluten allergy. If that's you, this isn't the safe option you're hoping for, and I'd rather tell you that upfront than have you find out the hard way. It's built for people choosing to reduce gluten, not those who must eliminate it completely.

What You Actually Get

Setting expectations aside, the crust itself is solid. It comes in a Small (10-inch) only — no medium, no large — and the texture is firm and crisp, closer to a thin crust than the pillowy Hand Tossed. A lot of people genuinely enjoy it and wouldn't guess it was gluten-free if you didn't tell them. As a Small, it's sized for one person, which suits a solo gluten-conscious diner nicely.

Price and How to Order

Expect a small upcharge over the standard crust, though as always it varies by location since Domino's is franchise-priced. You order it just like any pizza — pick Gluten Free as the crust, then add your toppings. Just keep in mind that the toppings and sauces aren't all guaranteed gluten-free, and everything shares the same kitchen, so read individual ingredients if you're sensitive.

Topping Tips for a Gluten-Conscious Order

Keep it simple. A classic cheese or pepperoni on the gluten-free crust is a safe, satisfying choice. Heavily processed or breaded add-ons are the ones to double-check. If you want to understand how this crust compares to the others in taste and texture, our crust types guide lays them all out side by side.

Who It's Really For

Think of the gluten-free crust this way. If you're gluten-sensitive or simply trying to cut back, it's a great, tasty option that lets you enjoy Domino's without the usual wheat load. If you have celiac disease or a serious allergy, it's not worth the risk, and you're better off with a dedicated gluten-free kitchen elsewhere. Knowing which camp you're in is the whole decision.

What "Shared Kitchen" Actually Means in Practice

The phrase gets used so often it stops meaning anything, so here is the concrete version. In a Domino's kitchen, over the life of a single shift:

  • Wheat flour is airborne. Regular dough is stretched and handled on the same counters all day, and flour does not stay where you put it
  • The same utensils move between pizzas — cutters, spatulas, pans
  • The oven is shared. Every pizza rides the same conveyor belt
  • Staff handle wheat dough and then handle toppings

None of that is negligence. It is simply how a high-volume pizza kitchen works, and no amount of care from the person making your pizza changes the underlying setup. Domino's is upfront about this, which is to its credit — the company explicitly says the crust is not recommended for people with celiac disease.

The practical translation: this is a reduced-gluten option, not a gluten-free-certified one. Those are different products aimed at different people.

Which Toppings and Sauces to Check

People focus entirely on the crust and forget that everything on top of it also has an ingredient list. Worth knowing where the risk sits:

ItemGenerally lower riskWorth checking
SauceStandard tomato sauceCreamy and BBQ style sauces
CheeseMozzarellaBlended and flavoured cheeses
MeatsPepperoni, hamBreaded chicken, meatballs, seasoned blends
VegetablesAll of them—

The rule that serves you best: the simpler the topping, the fewer surprises. Breaded items are the obvious ones to avoid — anything with a coating almost certainly involves wheat. A plain cheese or pepperoni pizza on the gluten-free crust is the cleanest order on the menu.

How It Compares to the Other Crusts

CrustSizesTextureContains wheat
Gluten FreeSmall onlyFirm, crisp, compactNo (shared kitchen)
Crunchy ThinS / M / LLight, cracker-likeYes
Hand TossedS / M / LSoft, chewyYes
Handmade PanS / MThick, butteryYes
Brooklyn StyleL / XLThin, foldableYes
Parmesan StuffedMediumFilled rimYes

Texture-wise, the closest comparison is Crunchy Thin — both are firm and crisp rather than soft. If you like thin crust generally, you will get on with this one. Our crust types guide covers all six in detail.

If You Still Want to Order It, Do This

For someone who is gluten-sensitive rather than celiac, a few steps genuinely reduce exposure:

  • Order at a quieter time. A slow mid-afternoon kitchen has less flour in the air than a Friday 7pm rush
  • Keep the toppings simple — cheese, pepperoni, plain vegetables
  • Add a note to the order asking for fresh gloves and a clean cutter. It is not a guarantee, but it costs nothing and many stores will accommodate it
  • Call the store and ask about their process. Practices vary between franchises more than people assume
  • Ask them not to cut it. The pizza cutter is one of the most shared pieces of equipment in the kitchen

That last one is the tip most people have never heard, and it removes a genuine contact point.

If You Have Celiac Disease

I want to be direct rather than diplomatic here, because this is a health question and hedging does not help you.

Domino's is not the right choice for celiac disease. Domino's says so itself. The steps above reduce risk; they do not eliminate it, and for celiac the standard is elimination, not reduction. A dedicated gluten-free kitchen — a pizzeria with separate prep areas, separate utensils and certification — is what that requires, and plenty of them exist.

There is no shame in ordering from Domino's for the rest of your household and eating something else yourself. That is a perfectly normal way to run a mixed-diet family, and it is safer than hoping a shared kitchen behaves differently tonight.

What It Costs

OrderSizeExample Price
Gluten-free cheese pizzaSmall 10\"~.99–.99
Gluten-free, one toppingSmall 10\"~.99–.99
Same pizza, Hand TossedSmall 10\"~.99–.99

Expect the gluten-free crust to carry a modest upcharge over the standard crust, typically a couple of dollars. Since it only comes in a small, you are also paying near-medium money for the least pizza on the menu — that is the real cost, more than the upcharge itself.

One thing worth checking before you pay: deals often exclude the gluten-free crust, or exclude the small size that it requires. Many promotions are built around medium and large pizzas, which rules it out by definition. Read the offer terms rather than assuming, and see our coupons page for what is currently running.

The Bottom Line

Domino's gluten-free crust is a genuinely good addition to the menu — crisp, enjoyable, and easy to order — as long as you go in with clear eyes about the shared-kitchen reality. This is an independent, unofficial guide, and allergen practices can change, so always confirm current preparation details with your store and verify prices at official checkout. For the rest of the menu, see our Domino's menu with prices.

faqs.question: What sides does Domino's have?
faqs.answer: Domino's sells bread sides (Parmesan Bread Bites, Garlic and Parmesan Bread Twists, Stuffed Cheesy Bread), Loaded Tots, chicken and wings, penne pasta in a dish or a bread bowl, oven-baked sandwiches, salads, desserts and dipping sauces. Nearly all of it comes out of the same conveyor oven the pizzas do.

faqs.question: How much is Domino's pasta?
faqs.answer: Around $6.99 to $7.99 for a pasta dish, and roughly $8.99 if you have it baked in a bread bowl. Chicken Alfredo, Chicken Carbonara, Italian Sausage Marinara, Pasta Primavera and a build-your-own penne are the usual options.

faqs.question: What is a Domino's bread bowl?
faqs.answer: A round loaf hollowed out and baked with your pasta inside it, so the bowl is edible. It costs roughly a dollar more than the same pasta in a dish and adds about 350 to 400 calories, because you are essentially ordering a large bread roll alongside your meal.

faqs.question: Does Domino's have Loaded Tots?
faqs.answer: Yes. Loaded Tots are potato tots baked with cheese and toppings, and they come in three versions: Cheddar Bacon, Melty 3-Cheese and Philly Cheese Steak. They are typically around $6.99 and are usually eligible for Mix & Match pricing.

faqs.question: How much are Domino's sandwiches?

faqs.question: What desserts does Domino's have?

faqs.question: Are Domino's sides included in the Mix & Match deal?
faqs.answer: Most of them, yes. Bread sides, Loaded Tots, pasta, sandwiches, chicken and desserts are typically eligible when you order two or more items at the Mix & Match price, which is usually cheaper than buying a side on its own.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest side at Domino's?
faqs.answer: Parmesan Bread Bites are usually the cheapest at around $4.99, and you get 16 pieces, which makes them the best value per piece of anything in the bread category.

faqs.question: Does Domino's have salads?
faqs.answer: Yes, though the range is small — usually a Classic Garden Salad and a Chicken Caesar, at around $6.99. They are packaged cold with dressing on the side, and the dressing is where most of the calories sit.

faqs.question: Which Domino's side has the fewest calories?
faqs.answer: A garden salad with the dressing used sparingly, followed by plain boneless chicken at roughly 50 calories a piece. Among the bread sides, a small portion of Parmesan Bread Bites is the lightest way in at about 220 calories for four.

content:
There's a Whole Menu Behind the Pizza

Most people open the Domino's app, order a pizza, maybe add whatever side the app pushes at checkout, and leave. Fair enough — it's a pizza place. But there's a genuinely large menu sitting behind that pizza: bread sides, Loaded Tots, pasta, oven-baked sandwiches, salads and desserts, most of it coming out of the same conveyor oven your pizza does.

Some of it is excellent value. Some of it quietly doubles your bill for food nobody at the table asked for. I've spent a long time working out which is which, so this guide walks the entire non-pizza menu with example prices, calories and a straight answer on what's worth ordering. As always on this site, prices are examples — Domino's stores are individually franchised, so confirm the real total at checkout.

Bread & Sides

This is the biggest category and the one people default to. Here's the lineup.

SidePortionExample PriceCalories
Parmesan Bread Bites16 pieces~$4.99~220 / 4 pc
Garlic Bread Twists8 pieces~$5.99~220 / 2 pc
Parmesan Bread Twists8 pieces~$5.99~230 / 2 pc
Stuffed Cheesy Bread8 pieces~$7.99~260 / 2 pc

Two things worth knowing here. First, Parmesan Bread Bites are the best value per piece on the whole menu — sixteen pieces for around five dollars, and they're the easiest thing to share around a table without anyone fighting over portions.

Second, a full order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread runs north of 1,000 calories. It's delicious, and I order it, but it is genuinely a main course dressed up as a side. If it's going on the order, drop a couple of slices of pizza rather than treating it as an extra — the full calorie picture for everything is in our Domino's calories and nutrition guide.

Loaded Tots — The Newest Side

Loaded Tots are the newest thing in this part of the menu: crispy potato tots baked with sauce and cheese on top, in three versions.

Loaded TotsWhat's On ThemCalories (per quarter)
Cheddar BaconBacon, mozzarella, cheddar, garlic Parmesan sauce~240 cal
Melty 3-CheeseMozzarella, cheddar, provolone, Alfredo~210 cal
Philly Cheese SteakSteak, onions, green peppers, Alfredo, cheese blend~200 cal

They're usually around $6.99 as part of a Mix & Match order. The honest verdict: they travel worse than bread does. Tots are at their best straight out of the oven, and a twenty-minute delivery takes the edge off the crispiness. Order them on carryout and they're a genuinely good side; order them on a long delivery and you may wonder what the fuss was about. Our carryout deals guide covers where pickup wins on price too.

Pasta: Dish or Bread Bowl

Domino's bakes penne pasta to order, and you choose how it's served — in a dish, or inside a hollowed-out bread bowl.

PastaIn a DishIn a Bread Bowl
Pasta Primavera~$7.99 · ~530–550 cal~$8.99 · varies
Chicken Alfredo~$6.99 · ~620 cal~$8.99 · ~690 cal
Italian Sausage Marinara~$6.99 · ~690 cal~$8.99 · ~730 cal
Chicken Carbonara~$7.99 · ~690 cal~$8.99 · varies
Build Your Own Penne~$7.99~$8.99

The bread bowl costs roughly a dollar more and, contrary to what you would expect, adds much less than a loaf of bread's worth of calories — published figures show Chicken Alfredo at about 620 in a dish against 690 in a bowl. The portion of pasta inside a bowl appears to be smaller, which offsets the bread. It is a fun novelty, the calorie penalty is mild, and the honest answer on whether it is worth a dollar is that it depends on how hungry you are.

Oven-Baked Sandwiches

These are the most overlooked thing on the menu, and they're the reason Domino's works as a lunch stop rather than just a dinner one.

SandwichExample Price
Philly Cheese Steak~$6.99–$8.99
Chicken Bacon Ranch~$6.99–$8.99
Chicken Habanero~$6.99–$8.99
Buffalo Chicken~$6.99–$8.99
Mediterranean Veggie~$8.99

They're baked on artisan bread in the same oven as the pizzas, which is why they arrive properly hot rather than sitting under a lamp. On calories, the three differ more than you would expect: Mediterranean Veggie is around 680–700, Philly Cheese Steak about 720, and Chicken Bacon Ranch roughly 870 — that's an approximate band rather than a precise figure, so check the app if it matters to you. For one person eating alone, a sandwich is often a smarter buy than a small pizza: similar money, no leftovers, and it survives the trip better.

Salads

The salad range is small and it isn't pretending otherwise — usually a Classic Garden Salad and a Chicken Caesar, around $6.99 each, packed cold with dressing on the side.

They do the job when one person in the group isn't eating pizza. The thing to watch is the dressing: it's a separate packet and it can carry more calories than the salad it's going on, so use half if you're being careful. Treat the salad as a side for someone who wants one, not as the reason you ordered.

Desserts

Short list, but the lava cakes have a genuine following.

DessertPortionExample PriceCalories
Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes2 cakes~$4.99~350 each
Cinnamon Bread Twists8 pieces~$5.99~250 / 2 pc
Marbled Cookie Brownie9 pieces~$6.99~200 / piece

The lava cakes are the pick. They come out warm with a molten centre, they're the cheapest dessert on the list, and two of them split neatly between two people. Cinnamon Bread Twists are the better choice for a group because there are eight pieces to go around, and the Marbled Cookie Brownie is the one to order when you want dessert to feed four or five without buying multiples.

Dipping Sauces

Small item, worth thirty seconds of your attention. Marinara is around 45 calories a cup; the creamy dips run roughly 100 to 170, and the garlic butter style dips are the heaviest of the lot. Dips are usually a dollar or so each, and they're the single easiest place to add calories you'd never think to count. If you're having two or three cups with a bread side, that's a meaningful number sitting quietly next to your pizza.

Which Sides Are Actually Worth It

Here's my honest ranking after a lot of ordering.

  • Best value: Parmesan Bread Bites — 16 pieces for around $4.99 and easy to share
  • Best for a group: Cinnamon Bread Twists or the Marbled Cookie Brownie — they divide properly
  • Best solo meal: an oven-baked sandwich — no leftovers, travels well
  • Best treat: Stuffed Cheesy Bread, as long as it replaces pizza rather than joining it
  • Best on carryout only: Loaded Tots — crispiness doesn't survive a long delivery
  • Think twice: the bread bowl upgrade, which is a dollar and 350+ calories for bread you already have on the table

How Sides Fit Into the Deals

This is where the money is, and it's the part most people miss.

Nearly all of these sides are Mix & Match eligible. That means when you order two or more qualifying items, each one drops to the deal price — and a side bought inside Mix & Match is almost always cheaper than the same side bought on its own alongside a full-price pizza. The mistake is ordering one pizza at menu price and then bolting a side on at menu price too.

Two practical moves. First, if you're buying a pizza and a side anyway, build the whole order inside the deal rather than adding the side at the end. Second, check whether two medium pizzas plus a side inside the deal costs less than one large plus a side outside it — surprisingly often, it does. Our Mix & Match explainer walks through the mechanics, the coupons page has what's live right now, and the money-saving playbook covers the rest of the levers.

Ordering for a Group

A quick rule that has never let me down: one shared side per three or four people, not one side per person. Sides at Domino's are portioned generously and they're all bread-based or cheese-heavy, so ordering three of them alongside pizza means most of it goes home in a box.

If you're feeding a mixed group, one bread side plus one dessert covers the whole table better than two bread sides. Add chicken or wings if you need something that isn't carbohydrate, and a couple of drinks from the fridge case rather than the 2-litre bottle if people want different things. Our family ordering guide has the pizza side of that equation.

The Short Version

The non-pizza menu at Domino's is bigger and better than its reputation. Bread Bites are the value pick, sandwiches are the underrated solo meal, lava cakes are the dessert to get, and the bread bowl is the upgrade to skip. Order the sides inside a deal rather than beside one, keep it to one or two shared items, and you'll eat better for less than the people ordering a pizza each and adding whatever the checkout screen suggests.

The full lineup with example prices by category is on our Domino's menu with prices page — and the checkout screen is still the only price that counts.

content:
The Chicken Menu People Underrate

Everyone goes to Domino's for pizza, sure. But the chicken menu is quietly one of the smartest ways to round out an order, and a genuinely good lighter meal on its own. There are three lanes here — boneless, wings, and specialty chicken — and they each do something different. Let me walk you through all of them so you order the right one for the right moment.

Boneless Chicken — The Versatile Workhorse

This is the one I'd tell most people to start with. Boneless Chicken is breaded, oven-baked, all-white-meat pieces — no bones, no mess. Order it plain with a dip and it's reasonable at roughly 50 calories a piece, or toss it in a sauce for more punch. An 8-piece runs around $8.99, and it's a top pick in a Mix & Match deal because it adds protein to a pizza order without costing much.

Wings — The Classic Bone-In

If you want the real deal, the bone-in wings deliver. Hot Buffalo is the timeless tangy choice, and BBQ brings the sweet-smoky side. An 8-piece order is usually about $9.49. Wings are messier and a little higher in calories than boneless — roughly 440 for a plain 8-piece, climbing to around 520 for Hot Buffalo and 560 for Sweet BBQ — but for a game night or a wing craving, nothing else scratches the itch quite the same way.

Specialty Chicken — The Loaded Option

This is Domino's most creative chicken idea and a lot of people have never tried it. Specialty Chicken takes boneless pieces and loads them with toppings and sauces like a little appetizer. The flavors are worth knowing.

Specialty ChickenWhat's On It
Crispy Bacon & TomatoBacon, tomato, a cheesy blend
Classic Hot BuffaloBuffalo sauce, cheese
Spicy Jalapeño-PineappleSweet heat, jalapeño, pineapple
Sweet BBQ BaconBBQ sauce, bacon, cheese

It eats like a knife-and-fork snack rather than finger food, and it's a nice change of pace from plain wings.

Pick Your Sauce

Sauce makes the order. For a mixed group, get boneless plain and let everyone dip their own way. Solo, pick a bold one — Sweet BBQ and Hot Buffalo are the crowd favorites, while Mango Habanero brings sweet-then-spicy heat. Just note the sweeter sauces add sugar and calories, so factor that in if you're watching intake.

Nutrition & Allergens, Straight

Plain boneless chicken is the lightest way in. Wings and sauced options climb in calories and sodium. Across the board, the breading contains wheat, milk, soy and egg, and everything's made in a shared kitchen, so none of it is gluten-free. If allergens matter to you, check current ingredient details with your store.

How to Order It Smart

Chicken shines as a deal add-on. Pair boneless with a pepperoni pizza and a drink through Mix & Match, or use it as the protein in a lighter meal alongside a thin-crust veggie pizza. Feeding a crowd? Wings plus Stuffed Cheesy Bread makes a proper spread. The full lineup and prices live on the menu with prices page.

Prices and Calories at a Glance

Here is the whole chicken range in one table so you can compare properly.

ItemPortionExample PriceCalories
Boneless Chicken (plain)8 pieces~$8.99~400
Boneless Chicken (plain)16 pieces~$15.99~800
Plain Wings8 pieces~$9.49~440
Hot Buffalo Wings8 pieces~$9.49~520
Sweet BBQ Wings8 pieces~$9.49~560
Specialty Chicken1 order~$7.99Varies by topping

Two things worth pulling out of that. Boneless is roughly 50 calories a piece; bone-in wings are around 55 plain and 65 to 70 sauced. And sauce is not a rounding error — the gap between plain wings and Sweet BBQ is about 120 calories across an 8-piece order, purely from what is brushed on top.

Boneless or Wings?

This is the actual decision most people are making, so here it is straight.

BonelessBone-in Wings
MessLow — fork or fingersHigh — bones, napkins
Calories (8 pc, plain)~400~440
Meat per pieceConsistentVaries
Best forKids, sharing, adding to a pizza orderGame night, wing cravings
Sauce coverageEven, breading holds itPatchy but classic

Boneless wins on practicality; wings win on occasion. If the chicken is going alongside pizza as part of a shared spread, boneless is the easier order — no bone pile, no wet wipes, and children can handle it. If wings are the point of the evening, nothing else does the job.

Sauce Guide

Sauce is where most of the character comes from, and the heat levels are not obvious from the names.

SauceHeatNotes
PlainNoneLightest option; pair with a dip
Garlic ParmesanNoneSavoury and rich rather than hot
Sweet BBQNoneSweetest, and the highest in calories
Hot BuffaloMediumThe classic tangy heat
Mango HabaneroHotSweet first, then a real burn

A practical trick for a mixed group: order plain and buy dips separately. Everyone sauces their own, nobody is stuck with heat they did not want, and the dips cost less than upgrading the whole order.

How Much to Order for a Group

The most common mistake here is under-ordering chicken and over-ordering pizza.

  • 2 people: one 8-piece alongside a medium pizza
  • 3–4 people: one 16-piece boneless, or two 8-piece orders in different sauces
  • 5+ people: two 16-piece orders, and expect them to go before the pizza does
  • As a meal on its own: an 8-piece plus a side feeds one person properly

Chicken disappears faster than pizza at a table because people take pieces absent-mindedly. If you are feeding a crowd, budget more than feels necessary.

Dips Matter More Than You Think

The dipping cup is the invisible part of the order. Marinara is around 45 calories a cup; ranch and blue cheese run roughly 100 to 170. If you are having two or three cups with an 8-piece, the dips can add as much as a couple of extra pieces of chicken would.

That is not a reason to skip them — it is a reason to know. Marinara is the light choice if you want one without thinking about it. Full numbers across the menu are in our calories and nutrition guide.

Chicken as the Whole Meal

Almost everything written about Domino's chicken treats it as a side, but it works perfectly well as the main event — and for one person it is often the better order.

MealExample PriceCalories
8-pc boneless + marinara~.99~445
Small cheese pizza~.99~1,200

Same money, and the chicken is around a third of the calories. If you are eating alone and want something hot that is not a carbohydrate brick, an 8-piece with a dip is a genuinely sensible dinner. Add a garden salad and it is a balanced one.

The other use case worth knowing: chicken is the protein that rescues a pizza order for someone tracking macros. Two slices of thin-crust veggie plus a few pieces of plain boneless lands far better nutritionally than four slices of pepperoni, for similar money and a similar amount of food on the plate.

The Bottom Line

Boneless for versatility and value, wings for the classic craving, specialty chicken when you want something different. Domino's chicken is better than most people give it credit for, especially inside a deal. title: Domino's Carryout Deals Guide (2026): The Cheapest Way to Order
excerpt: Carryout is the quiet money-saver at Domino's. Here's how the carryout deals work, why they beat delivery every time, and how to build the cheapest possible order.
author: amna-sadam
imageAlt: A Domino's carryout order ready for pickup

faqs.question: Is carryout cheaper than delivery at Domino's?
faqs.answer: Yes, consistently. Carryout skips the delivery fee (typically $4–6) and any tip, and it often unlocks pickup-only specials that delivery orders can't get. It's the cheapest way to order, full stop.

faqs.question: What is the Domino's carryout special?
faqs.answer: Domino's regularly runs a carryout-only deal on large pizzas at a low fixed price. The exact price and terms rotate, so check the deals tab in the app before ordering.

faqs.question: Do I still get deals if I pick up?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Mix & Match, $6.99 Each and carryout-only specials all apply to pickup orders — and you avoid the delivery fee on top.
