faqs.question: Is carryout faster than delivery?
faqs.answer: Often, yes — you skip the driver's route entirely. Once the tracker shows your order is ready, it's a quick in-and-out.

content:
The Cheapest Trick That Isn't Really a Trick

Want to know the single easiest way to spend less at Domino's? Go pick it up. That's it. Carryout is the quiet money-saver that most people walk right past because delivery is so convenient. But if your couch can survive a ten-minute round trip, carryout will genuinely save you money on basically every order. Let me show you exactly why, and how to squeeze the most out of it.

Why Carryout Wins on Price

Two reasons, and together they're decisive. First, you skip the delivery fee entirely — that's four to six dollars gone before you even think about a tip. Second, Domino's regularly runs carryout-only specials, like a low fixed price on large pizzas, that delivery orders simply can't access. So you're saving on the fee and unlocking exclusive pricing. It's not a small edge, it's the biggest easy saving on the whole menu.

CarryoutDelivery
Delivery fee$0$4–6
TipNone neededRecommended
Exclusive dealsPickup-only specialsFewer
SpeedOften fasterDepends on route

The Carryout Special

The headliner is Domino's carryout-only large pizza deal — a low fixed price you won't see on delivery. The exact number and terms rotate, so peek at the deals tab in the app before you order. When it's live, it's one of the best value pizzas going, and stacking it with your own toppings choices keeps it cheap.

Stack It With Other Deals

Here's where carryout gets really powerful — it combines with everything. Order through Mix & Match or $6.99 Each, pick carryout, and you get the deal price with zero delivery fee. Stay signed into Domino's Rewards and you're still earning points toward a free pizza. That's three savings layers on one order, and it's exactly the routine I recommend in the money-saving guide.

How to Order Carryout Smart

Open the app, build your order around a deal, and select carryout at checkout. The tracker shows when it's ready so you're not standing around the store. A quick tip: order a large over a medium since the per-slice value is better, and grab a 2-liter instead of individual bottles for the cheapest drinks.

When Delivery Still Makes Sense

I'm not anti-delivery — sometimes it's the right call. Bad weather, no car, a house full of people you can't leave, or you simply want the comfort of not moving. That convenience has a price, and that's fine when you choose it knowingly. But for pure value, carryout wins every single time, and it's worth defaulting to it whenever you reasonably can.

The Real Cost Difference, Worked Out

Percentages are easy to wave away, so here is an actual order priced both ways. Say you want a large pepperoni and an order of Stuffed Cheesy Bread — an extremely normal Friday.

Line itemCarryoutDelivery
Large pepperoni~$12.99~$12.99
Stuffed Cheesy Bread~$7.99~$7.99
Delivery fee$0~$4.99
Tip (customary ~15%)$0~$3.15
Before tax~$20.98~$29.12

That is roughly eight dollars on a twenty-one dollar order — about 39% more to have the same food carried to your door. Order that way once a week and you are spending somewhere near $400 a year on the convenience.

None of that is an argument that delivery is a rip-off. It is an argument that the gap is much bigger than most people picture, and worth knowing before you default to it.

The Fees Nobody Mentions

Two things about delivery pricing genuinely surprise people, and both are worth understanding.

The delivery fee is not a tip. This is the big one. That $4 to $6 charge is a store fee — it does not go to the driver as wages in the way customers often assume. Which means the tip sits on top of it rather than being covered by it. If you have been skipping tips because "the delivery fee covers it," that is the misunderstanding worth correcting.

Some stores price the delivery menu differently. Because every Domino's is independently franchised, a store can set different prices for delivery orders than for carryout. It is not universal, but it happens. The easy way to check yours: build the same order twice in the app, switching between carryout and delivery, and compare the subtotal before fees. If the subtotal itself moves, your store does this.

How Long Carryout Actually Takes

The honest answer is that carryout is often faster than delivery, which is the part people get wrong.

  • Baking time is identical either way — your pizza takes the same few minutes in the oven
  • Delivery adds a queue — your order waits for a driver, who may be running two or three other stops on the same route
  • Carryout skips that entirely — the pizza is ready when it is ready

On a busy Friday night the difference can be substantial. The tracker in the app tells you when your order is ready, so the trick is simple: order first, then leave. Do not drive over and stand in the store waiting — place it from home, watch the tracker, and time your arrival.

Which Orders Save the Most

Carryout is always cheaper, but the size of the win varies more than you would expect.

Order typeRoughly how much you save
One small pizzaMost — the fee is a huge share of a small total
Pizza plus a sideA lot — fee plus tip on a mid-size order
Large family orderLeast, proportionally — the fee is a smaller slice

The counterintuitive takeaway: carryout matters most on small orders. On a $10 pizza, a $5 delivery fee plus tip can nearly double what you pay. On a $60 family order it is a rounding error by comparison. If you are ordering solo, this is the single biggest saving available to you.

Five Carryout Mistakes

Things I see people do that quietly give the saving back:

  • Not checking the deals tab first. Carryout-only specials rotate, and the best one is often not the one advertised on the home screen.
  • Driving over before ordering. You end up waiting in the store for the full bake time instead of at home.
  • Forgetting to sign in. No sign-in, no rewards points — and points are a free pizza you already paid for.
  • Ordering a medium when a large is inside the deal. The per-slice value on a large is nearly always better; see our sizes guide.
  • Adding items at menu price after building the deal. Put everything inside the offer instead of bolting a side on at the end.

Carryout Also Tastes Better

This gets left out of the money conversation, and it shouldn't. Pizza starts declining the moment it leaves the oven, and the decline is mostly about steam. Sealed in a cardboard box, moisture comes out of the pizza, hits the lid and goes straight back into the crust. Fifteen minutes of that and the base has gone soft.

Carryout typically cuts that window in half. You are collecting the pizza minutes after it leaves the belt rather than after a driver has completed a route with two other stops. The crust is crisper, the cheese has not congealed, and anything fried or breaded is dramatically better.

Some items barely survive delivery at all. Loaded Tots are the clearest example — crispiness is the entire point and steam destroys it. Chocolate Lava Crunch Cakes are the other: the molten centre sets as they cool, so a long delivery turns them into ordinary chocolate cake. If either is in your order, carryout is not just cheaper, it is a different product.

The Bottom Line

Carryout is the least glamorous and most reliable way to save at Domino's. Skip the fee, grab a pickup-only special, stack a deal and rewards on top, and you'll consistently pay less than the person ordering the same food to their door.
